articles.title: Russell Brand accused by 6 women of sexual misconduct, assault following rape conviction
articles.summary: Six more women have come forward alleging sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by ex-comedian Russell Brand, according to an investigation by the U.K.-based The Times, following his conviction…

image.caption: More allegations of sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour have been made against former comedian and actor Russell Brand, shown at Southwark Crown Court in London on Nov. 2, in the wake of his criminal conviction for rape and sexual assault. (Alberto Pezzali/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Six more women have come forward alleging sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by ex-comedian Russell Brand, according to an investigation by the U.K.-based The Times, following his conviction on rape and sexual assault earlier this week.
An investigation by The Times details further allegations against ex-comedian
WARNING: This article may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.

Six more women have come forward alleging sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by Russell Brand, according to an investigation by the U.K.-based newspaper The Times, following his conviction for rape and sexual assault earlier this week.

The 51-year-old former comedian and actor was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday after being found guilty of raping a woman and committing three sexual assaults between 2004 and 2009.
In a joint investigation by The Times and Sunday Times published Friday, six more women described non-consensual encounters with Brand, including rape and sexual harassment.
The publication also coincided with the release of a Netflix documentary on Brand called Open Secret, which examines how rumours of his unsettling behaviour persisted throughout his career.

One woman told The Times that Brand had continued having sex with her after she noticed he wasn't wearing a condom and told him to stop. She said the assault occurred during an on-off relationship she had with the actor in the late 2000s, and that Brand texted her to apologize afterwards.
"I justified it in my head by saying to myself: at least he admitted it," she told The Times.
Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison
Another woman, who said she met Brand while lining up at one of his gigs in 2007 when she was 19, said she told him during a sexual encounter she was in pain but that he continued anyway.
"And then it gets worse and it's really painful. And I say 'stop' and he doesn't stop," she said.

items: Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on convictions for rape, sexual assaults

blocks.text: She alleged that Brand told her afterwards: "Tonight was consensual. Nobody did anything they didn’t want to do."
"And that's the moment I just thought ... I know that you know what you've done is wrong," she said.
Russell Brand sentenced: The CBC's Andrew Nichols talks with columnist Katie Glass of The Times
Many of the women described meeting Brand at his comedy gigs or in situations where they felt he used his celebrity to manipulate them into hotel rooms, where his demeanour then changed.

One woman told The Times she was shocked by how quickly he changed from the "affable, charming, sort of dandyish persona" he initially appeared to be to a "really crude and direct person" in his hotel room, where she alleges he abruptly groped her and shoved his hand down her pants.
"At the time, I never really thought about it in the way that I think about it now, as sexual assault. I just pushed it down," she said.

items: Russell Brand denies all charges as he takes the stand at rape and sex assault trial

blocks.text: CBC News has reached out to Brand's lawyer for comment.
The Times reported that several women it interviewed reported they feared they wouldn't be believed if they came forward — echoing fears raised by the woman who testified against him at his trial.
One of Brand's victims, whom he anally raped in 2009, said in a statement read by prosecutors in court that "his fame, wealth and influence created a power imbalance, which made me feel powerless."
Allegations emerged against Brand in 2023

Brand first rose to prominence on the comedy circuit in the U.K. in the late 1990s. He became more well known overseas after appearing in movie comedies such as Forgetting Sarah Marshall, Get Him to the Greek and Arthur, and engaging in a highly publicized, if brief, marriage to singer Katy Perry.

Allegations of sexual misconduct against Brand were first reported by The Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches in 2023. After these allegations became public, more women came forward to speak with police and media, and London's Metropolitan Police opened an investigation.
Brand poses alongside his then-fiancée, singer Katy Perry, at the premiere of the film Get Him to the Greek, at the Greek Theater in Los Angeles in 2010. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

Brand denied all charges during the recent four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London, maintaining that any sexual encounters were consensual and describing himself as preoccupied with sex during the years in question.
He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Brand is still under investigation for two other alleged rapes, one involving a then-16-year-old girl, according to police.
Russell Brand trial judge: 'You had also become a sexual predator'
Documentary dives into Brand's rise to fame

Friday also saw the release of the Netflix documentary Open Secret, which tracks Brand's career from his success on the stage as a controversial comedian known for bawdy jokes, to his acting roles and eventual shift into a far-right religious influencer — unfolding amid growing rumours that his unnerving persona might cloak real-life atrocities.
Jordan Martin, an ex-girlfriend who appeared in the documentary, described Brand as controlling and abusive, alleging that he sexually assaulted her after an argument.

The documentary by 72 Films includes archival footage from early comedy shows and appearances, including an on-stage Q&A in which he described himself as a "bloke from Essex," before adding, "I also raped someone once."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: Alberta's top court overturns certification for class-action lawsuit over COVID restrictions
articles.summary: Alberta’s top court has overturned the certification of a class-action lawsuit filed by a group of business owners who were seeking compensation for losses suffered due to pandemic-related public…

image.caption: Whistle Stop Cafe owner Christopher Scott, left, was one of the named plaintiffs in a lawsuit that sought compensation from the Alberta government due to COVID-related public health restrictions. The lawsuit was filed by lawyer Jeffrey Rath, right. On Friday, the Alberta Court of Appeal overturned t

blocks.text: Calgary·New

Alberta’s top court has overturned the certification of a class-action lawsuit filed by a group of business owners who were seeking compensation for losses suffered due to pandemic-related public health restrictions and closures.
Alberta business owners hurt by pandemic restrictions sued province for losses
In a 17-page decision issued Friday, the panel of three Alberta Court of Appeal judges ruled that the lawsuit is “bound to fail.”

The proposed class action — headed by gym owner Rebecca Ingram and Whistle Stop Cafe owner Christopher Scott as representative plaintiffs — was certified in 2024 by Court of King’s Bench Justice Colin Feasby.

The lawsuit, filed by lawyer Jeffrey Rath, followed the superior court’s 2023 “Ingram” decision in which Justice Barbara Romaine found that Alberta’s health orders were made outside the scope of the province's Public Health Act, which requires the chief medical officer of health (CMOH) to make public health orders.
'Fail to disclose causation'

Romaine found that while the CMOH made recommendations and ultimately implemented restrictions, it was cabinet and committees that had the final decision making power. The orders were otherwise found to be constitutional.

items: Role of politicians in pandemic restriction decision-making breached Alberta Public Health Act: Calgary judge

blocks.text: Rath's lawsuit alleged that because the orders were found to be unlawful, Alberta is liable for the losses suffered by class members due to closures and restrictions imposed on businesses.

Alberta appealed the certification, and on Friday, the appeal panel sided with the government, finding that the alleged negligent conduct relates to the procedure, not the substance of the CMOH orders.
“If the identical CMOH Orders had been issued by the Chief Medical Officer … there would be no negligent act and no claim,” wrote the panel.

“The class action pleadings fail to disclose causation — that the alleged procedural defect caused injury to the class members … as a result of this fundamental flaw in the proposed claim, it is plain and obvious that it is bound to fail.”

During the pandemic, Scott faced several charges, accused of breaching the Public Health Act when his restaurant, the Whistle Stop Cafe in Mirror, Alta., remained open despite restrictions banning large gatherings and in-person dining in January 2021.
Scott's charges were stayed after Romaine's decision was released.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Meghan Grant is a justice affairs reporter. She has been covering courts, crime and stories of police accountability in southern Alberta for more than 15 years. Send Meghan a story tip at meghan.grant@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Andy Burnham urges Labour to ‘re-arm’ for Kemi Badenoch comeback
articles.summary:
No 10 sources say PM wants party to refocus on Tories as electoral threat after prioritising Reform and Greens

Andy Burnham has instructed the Labour party to “re-arm” to fight the…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has instructed the Labour party to “re-arm” to fight the Conservatives at the next election amid concern inside government that they must take the prospect of a Kemi Badenoch-led recovery seriously.

Downing Street sources said the prime minister wanted Labour headquarters to refocus on the Tories as an electoral threat after more than two years of prioritising Nigel Farage’s Reform and – on their left flank – the Greens.

“Andy is well aware of how volatile electoral support is. Just because the Tories are trailing in the polls now, their trajectory is upwards and they could bounce back ahead of the election. We can’t be complacent about our old foe,” one source said.

The Conservatives took 24% of the vote at the last general election, before support dipped to 18%. But last week this had risen to 25%, according to polling from More in Common, the first time in 18 months they have exceeded their vote share at the time of their record election defeat.

Many Tory MPs, who had felt that their party’s situation was existential, now believe they have a route back, with Badenoch finally appearing to recognise that the economy, rather than culture wars, presents her with an opportunity, especially with her core vote.

A senior Downing Street figure said that Burnham did not want party officials to take their eyes off Reform – which has dipped in the polls amid ongoing scrutiny of party finances – but felt they should be planning for a potential Tory resurgence as well.

A third No 10 insider told the Guardian: “Kemi is running a party base strategy with policies aimed at higher earners, mostly in the south. It won’t be enough to win them at the next election but it does put them more in contention. We need to be ready for that. We need to re-arm.”

Cabinet ministers including transport secretary Heidi Alexander, chief secretary Emma Reynolds and Europe minister Hamish Falconer all have Tory-facing seats, while Labour MPs across Hertfordshire, Kent and parts of London, including Finchley and Harrow, could also be at risk.

One tactic under discussion is talking up the prospect of a Tory-Reform pact, with MPs suggesting voters would only return in earnest to the Tories if there was a genuine chance they could win a majority, but that they could stay Labour if they worried about Farage getting close to power.

Another is to focus on the Tory brand – including the shadow cabinet – more generally. While Badenoch’s personal ratings are relatively strong, the Conservatives overall lag way behind, with a third of people who told More in Common she was doing a good job, still saying they would not vote for her party.

Labour officials insisted that, as the Conservatives were the official opposition in parliament, they still had them in their sights day to day. But they acknowledged they needed to step up their strategy more generally.

The party is understood to be preparing to devote more resources to taking on the Tories from January, in the run-up to the next May elections. “We did really well at this set of elections last time, so it will be a real test point for whether the Tories have got their act together,” one said.

A group of London MPs has personally urged Burnham to refocus on Badenoch’s party, which in some polls has overtaken Reform into second place, warning him that Labour HQ was “getting caught out” by “obsessing” about Reform and the Greens.
One minister with a slim majority said they had been raising the alarm inside government about the need to refocus on the Conservatives.

“I have been banging this drum for a while. It’s time to wake up about it, frankly. I think lots of my colleagues under threat from Reform have seen some of us in more traditional Tory seats as having it easy but by the next election it could be the other way around.”

One former Keir Starmer staffer said: “Every arm of the Labour party has been refocused to take on Reform, all the strategic decisions have been taken with that in mind. That can change if the party starts the work now but it does need to start properly.”

Luke Tryl, director of More in Common, said that Burnham was right to broaden the party’s focus. “Starmer was fighting on one front, but Labour now has two fronts on its right flank. They need to prepare for all outcomes,” he said.
“Reform has shown an ability to squeeze the Conservatives but it definitely has limits, so they’re definitely going to be on the pitch at the next election.”

Tryl suggested that the biggest risk to Labour was “self-sorting” by voters, with Reform winning right-leaning votes from Labour in the “Red Wall”, while the Conservatives took them in affluent parts of England including the south-east.

“Because of the shallow but broad nature of Labour’s support at the last election, there are more seats that could end up being Labour-Tory fights than you might think,” he said, adding that the Tories were also currently taking more votes from the Lib Dems than the other way round.

articles.title: Labour chief whip takes tough approach in Vogue interview to keeping MPs in line
articles.summary:
Anneliese Midgley surprises colleagues after Burnham said whips office should not be ‘something to be feared’

If Andy Burnham has been accused of being a people pleaser by his critics, the…

blocks.text: If Andy Burnham has been accused of being a people pleaser by his critics, the same most certainly cannot be said of his chief whip.

“I’m not going to take any shit and I don’t fuck about,” said Anneliese Midgley, the Labour government’s newest head of party discipline, shedding some light on her direct approach to keeping MPs in line.

Midgley, the MP for Knowsley, who is one of the prime minister’s closest friends in government, has surprised some Labour MPs with her strikingly “frank yet glam” interview in Vogue in which she said she’s determined to win. She also highlighted her unlikely journey from a deprived Liverpool housing estate, via the arts world to the heart of government.
But it was her honesty in regards to being tough that caught attention from her Labour colleagues who hoped Burnham’s reign would be marked by an end to Starmer’s strict party management style.

Burnham wrote to MPs back in July: “I want to create a different culture where MPs are happy and fulfilled doing their jobs, where everyone has a part to play and where opinions and approaches are respected, even where there’s difference … the whips’ office should be our HR department, not something to be feared or where discipline is used to stifle debate.”

At the time many Labour MPs, particularly those on the party’s left wing breathed a sigh of relief until he appointed Midgley as his chief whip, with some even going as far as saying they would be in “her bad books” because “I’m not one of her buddies she hangs and drinks with on the parliamentary terrace”.

Midgley, who worked as Jeremy Corbyn’s deputy chief of staff and Keir Starmer’s senior special adviser, criticised the former prime minister’s approach to managing the parliamentary Labour party (PLP) and praised Burnham’s approach – a man she said she “would run through the walls for”.

On party discipline, Midgley said: “These are grown-ups who should be treated with absolute respect, who’ve got a wealth of ideas and advice – not just treated as a number to go through a voting lobby.”
When challenged on whether she thought Starmer treated MPs “as a number”, the chief whip replied: “Yeah, I do think that.” Midgley has also worked as Starmer’s senior special adviser.

Despite her celebration of Burnham’s collegiate approach, Midgley told the magazine: “I’m very determined. If there’s things I want to do, I will do them. Basically, I will win,” she said laughing, according to the magazine.
“Obviously, I said all of that stuff before about team-building, and that’s absolutely right. But like, I’m not going to take any shit and I don’t fuck about. Do you know what I mean?”

One MP described the interview as striking, not just because chief whip’s usually keep their heads down and far away from the spotlight, but because she managed to articulate herself as an MP bringing a new era into the “dark arts” of “chief whipping”, being one that has artistic taste, fashion sense and determination to rise from child poverty to being an influential minister.

The interview, appears to mark another way in which Burnham’s government are attempting to start a new phase in Labour politics, or simply making themselves appear more human, while “scaring the shit out of the PLP”, according to one senior Labour MP.

articles.title: Stelco recalling 175 laid-off workers at Hamilton steel plant
articles.summary: Hamilton steelmaker Stelco is recalling 175 workers that had been laid off earlier this fall.

image.caption: The Stelco Hamilton Works is pictured on Oct. 9, 2026. The company says it is recalling 175 laid-off workers by Dec. 1. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Politics·Breaking
Hamilton steelmaker Stelco is recalling 175 workers that had been laid off earlier this fall.
Federal government told company to recall workers or face possible legal action

Stelco made the announcement in a news release on Friday, saying that the workers would be back in the factory by Dec. 1. The company also indicated that it would retroactively pay the workers for the time they were laid off.
The American parent company, Cleveland-Cliffs, announced in September that it planned to lay off as many as 500 workers as it idled certain steel production at Stelco.
The federal government said that any move to lay off workers would violate "binding commitments" Cleveland-Cliffs made when it bought Stelco in 2024.
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly wrote to the Ohio-based company in mid-October, demanding that it reverse the layoffs or face possible legal action.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Avril Lavigne welcomes baby girl
articles.summary: Canadian pop-punk princess Avril Lavigne has welcomed her first child — a baby girl — with an unnamed partner.

image.caption: Avril Lavigne performs onstage during Avril Lavigne: The Greatest Hits at Madison Square Garden on May 30, 2025 in New York City. (Theo Wargo/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Canadian pop-punk princess Avril Lavigne has welcomed her first child — a baby girl — with an unnamed partner.
“Our Mini F--king Princess has arrived,” she wrote on social media

"Our Mini F--king Princess has arrived 🎀👑🍼🩷," Lavigne shared in a post on Instagram, accompanied by a carousel of photos, including her and her mystery partner holding the newborn's hand and a row of three classic checkered slip-on Vans — lined up in a row on a skateboard.
Lavigne, 42, hasn't revealed the baby's name or who her father is; the Sk8er Boi singer is not publicly linked to anyone at the moment.

Lavigne has been married twice in the past to fellow well-known Canadian musicians: Sum 41 frontman Deryck Whibley (2006–2010) and Nickelback's Chad Kroeger (2013–2015). She was also once engaged to American rapper Mod Sun, and has been previously linked to Tyga, Brandon Davis, Wilmer Valderrama and Brody Jenner.

Her latest release came in 2024 in the form of a career-spanning greatest hits album, including 20 songs across her seven studio albums — everything from Complicated to Girlfriend to Head Above Water.
Love Sux, her most recent studio album, was released in 2022 and produced by Mod Sun, Travis Barker and John Feldmann.

While Lavigne has not toured in 2026, she embarked on a 69-show Greatest Hits Tour starting in Vancouver in 2024. The run included 13 stops across Canada, concluding at the All Your Friends Festival in Oro-Medonte, Ont., in June 2025.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

articles.title: Feds, Ontario offering Stellantis 'aggressive package' to keep Brampton auto plant open
articles.summary: The federal and Ontario governments are mounting a last-ditch effort to save the Stellantis auto plant in Brampton by pitching the company possible survival "scenarios" and offering an "aggressive…

image.caption: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says the federal and Ontario governments are trying to stop the sale of the Stellantis auto plant in Brampton by offering the company an 'aggressive package' of support. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The federal and Ontario governments are mounting a last-ditch effort to save the Stellantis auto plant in Brampton by pitching the company possible survival "scenarios" and offering an "aggressive package" of support to make it happen.
Industry minister says funding for Brampton is contractually linked to Windsor plant
Rather than hold a news conference to announce this latest step, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly revealed the plan in Woodbridge, Ont., at another announcement.

"We've put an aggressive package to Stellantis to prevent the sale. And we are still in solution mode to prevent the sale," Joly said in response to a reporter's question about the future of the plant.

Joly said the next move is for her, Unifor — the union representing workers at the plant — and Ontario Minister of Economic Development Vic Fedeli to meet with Stellantis global CEO Antonio Filosa to pitch the plan.

items: Stellantis auto plant closure in Brampton a 'betrayal' to all Canadians, Carney says
Carney aware of 'some aspects' of Stellantis auto plant sale, but says company still broke deal

blocks.text: Fedeli said Unifor has come up with more than one scenario for how the sale can be stopped and the plant "kept warm" until new Stellantis product lines can return.

"They have brought forward some suggestions. These are men and women who have built products at Stellantis's Brampton plant for decades. They know exactly what needs to happen in that plant," Fedeli said.
$2.5B auto support package
In October, the federal and Ontario governments announced an $8.7-billion support package for steel, critical mineral and auto sectors, with $2.5 billion earmarked for the auto sector over two years.
Fedeli said the financial support for Unifor's suggested "scenarios" will be paid for out of that fund.
"Not all of it, of course, but part of it is available for this solution," Fedeli said.

items: Carney, Ford announce $8.7B partnership to support steel, auto, critical mineral sectors

blocks.text: In 2022, the Trudeau government promised to inject up to $529 million in Stellantis plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., to help them increase production of electric and gas-powered vehicles.

More than 2,000 workers at Stellantis's Brampton plant have been out of work since the company halted operations in 2023 to begin that retooling process so the facility could produce the Jeep Compass.
But Stellantis paused the retooling effort in early 2025, announcing in October of that year that the Jeep Compass would be built at the Belvidere Assembly Plant in Illinois instead.
Joly says feds have 'levers' around Stellantis plant sale — but not what they are
The plant's future in Brampton had been left in limbo until Monday, when Stellantis announced it was selling the facility to Canadian armoured ⁠vehicle maker Roshel Inc..
"When it comes to Stellantis our position is clear: they cannot close the plant," Joly said. "If they would, we would sue them … and they're on the hook for hundreds of millions of dollars."

Last December, CBC News confirmed that the federal government had given $222 million to the Canadian arm of Stellantis between 2023 and 2025. CBC News asked the federal government for the most recent total but has yet to receive a response.
But in a statement on Thursday, Stellantis Canada CEO Trevor Longley said the company will only return subsidies to the government to the tune of $24 million.

items: Feds say Stellantis owes 'hundreds of millions' in subsidies, company offers $24M

blocks.text: "Documents are clear, contracts also are clear. The Brampton facility of Stellantis is linked to the Windsor plant and also the battery investments, that's why I've said and I continue to say Stellantis is on the hook for hundreds of millions of dollars," Joly said Friday.

President of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association Flavio Volpe says that according to Stellantis's product plan, it still has four vehicles for the 2029 model year that have not been assigned to a plant.
"Let's stop the sale, keep the plant warm and then work on landing those products here," Volpe told CBC News.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Peter Zimonjic is a senior writer for CBC News who reports for digital, radio and television. He has worked as a reporter and columnist in London, England, for the Telegraph, Times and Daily Mail, and in Canada for the Ottawa Citizen, Torstar and Sun Media. He is the author of Into The Darkness: An Account of 7/7, published by Vintage.

articles.title: Mexico raises $5.4M for social services by selling off Ryan Wedding's motorbike collection
articles.summary: Mexico has raised roughly $5.4 million by auctioning off a rare collection of motorcycles seized from alleged Canadian drug lord Ryan Wedding, with the funds earmarked for social services.

image.caption: The FBI released pictures of motorcycles seized by Mexican law enforcement during raids targeting Ryan Wedding. On the right, Wedding is seen arriving in California following his arrest in January 2026. (FBI)

blocks.text: World·New
Mexico has raised roughly $5.4 million by auctioning off a rare collection of motorcycles seized from alleged Canadian drug lord Ryan Wedding, with the funds earmarked for social services.
Accused drug trafficker's motorcycles were seized last year, before Wedding's arrest and extradition to U.S.

Mexican authorities say a "historic" two-day bidding war has raised roughly $5.4 million through the sale of a rare collection of high-end motorcycles seized from alleged Canadian drug lord Ryan Wedding — with the funds earmarked for social services.
The Ontario-born alleged cocaine kingpin's motorbike collection was uncovered in law enforcement raids last year in Mexico City and the nearby Mexico state.

Wedding's collection of rare and high-performance motorcycles — which include models from Ducati, Honda, Kawasaki, MV Agusta, Suzuki and Yamaha — were estimated by the FBI to be worth roughly $40 million US after they were seized in December.

More than a hundred attendees at a banquet hall south of Mexico City waited in anticipation Wednesday for the public bidding to open on hundreds of items, which included the dozens of luxury motorbikes belonging to the former Canadian Olympic athlete, according to reporting from the newspaper El País.

Speaking to reporters alongside Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum this morning, the head of the Mexican public agency INDEP — translated as the institute to return stolen assets to the people — described the two-day bidding war on Wednesday and Thursday as "historic."
Motorcycles seized from Ryan Wedding used for pro racing: FBI
Mónica Fernández Balboa said some of the "impressive" motorcycles "are going to museums in other parts of the world."
She said 57 of Wedding's 62 seized motorbikes were sold, with the remaining five to be auctioned off on Nov. 27.
Of the $5.4 million Cdn raised, Sheinbaum said $3 million would go toward a music conservatory. Proceeds from the agency's auctions typically go to fund social services.
El País said bidders at the Wednesday auction ranged from private enthusiasts to a well-known U.S. collecting and auction house.
Mexican authorities opened up a public bidding war on 61 motorcycles — including this one — earlier this week. The machines were seized in December 2025 during raids targeting Wedding. (INDEP)
At the time, Wedding was considered one of the agency's most wanted fugitives.
He was arrested the following month.
Wedding's California-based lawyer, Anthony Colombo, described the auction as a "corrupt action by Mexican law enforcement" in an email to CBC News ahead of the auction.
He said the bikes were found as part of a U.S. investigation and American authorities had not sought to seize the property. Colombo said Mexico had no authority to claim the goods.
"Any buyer of this property should be aware that they are not purchasing an item with a clear title and will be subject to litigation regarding ownership in the future," Colombo said.
With files from Thomas Daigle and Sara Jabakhanji

articles.title: No 10 considering expanding under-25s benefits overhaul to older age groups
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Plans to replace key disability benefits for young people with work and training could affect adults

Downing Street is considering whether plans to replace key disability benefits…

blocks.text: Downing Street is considering whether plans to replace key disability benefits for the under-25s with work and training should be expanded to older age groups, the Guardian has learned, in a move that risks reigniting Labour tensions over welfare changes.

The prime minister and other cabinet ministers are looking at applying the idea of “participation first” to all working ages, meaning spending billions more on support to enter the workplace while cutting or removing some disability benefits.

The move would be a risky political one given the difficulties that Keir Starmer faced with getting changes to health and disability benefits past the Labour parliamentary party last year, with a rebellion leading to a major U-turn.

The discussion on changing disability benefits for over-25s comes as the government prepares to accept recommendations from its adviser, Alan Milburn, next week on overhauling the system for young people.

In his report, Milburn will propose that under-25s should get training and support instead of the universal credit health element. Under the plans, young people with disabilities will also lose their personal independence payment (Pip) but will be able to apply to a local fund for specific short-term expenses and equipment – rather than an ongoing payment. Those with the most extreme needs who cannot work will have their entitlements protected.

Ahead of the Milburn review, cabinet ministers have this week looked at whether the arguments can be more broadly applied to over-25s, and are considering an intervention from the prime minister or Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, to make the case that the same principles should apply to all. This could take place within weeks after both the Milburn review and the Stephen Timms review into disability benefits have been published.

Some government sources believe the idea of expanding the welfare reforms to over-25s will ultimately not survive given the probable backlash from some parts of Labour but others believe Milburn has successfully made the case that the system needs to be changed and that the public are behind his efforts.
Andy Burnham has repeatedly emphasised that the changes will not be “crude cuts” but some backbenchers are sceptical and worried about the impact on young disabled people.

If the changes are expanded in principle to the over-25s, it could yield more savings as the cohort is much larger than the under- 25s and the level of support needed to get people back into employment would probably be at a lower level.

Ministers also believe that any system for the over-25s would need to reflect the different circumstances of older people, many of whom have families or caring responsibilities, and more complex health needs. However, there is a belief that many of the core problems of detachment from the workplace and a need to encourage greater participation are the same for both under and over-25s.

A government source said: “The support offer and benefit changes Alan has set out were devised for young people and the specific circumstances they face. But the Timms review has set out that Pip is no longer fit for purpose and the government will respond to that review when it reports.”

Milburn, a former cabinet minister under Tony Blair, has promised his report is about giving billions more in support to young people to help them into the workplace. But the Guardian has also learned there has been consternation within some government departments – including the Department of Health and the Department for Education – about where the upfront funding for Milburn’s extra support will come from within their budgets.

Some estimates have put the level of support Milburn is proposing at about £6bn. However, it is understood that the government will not put that level of spending on support that will be provided to young people instead of benefits – although there will be some numbers provided about different elements of funding required and a trajectory to savings.

Milburn told the Guardian earlier this week that the support for young people outlined in his report would create 440,000 employment and education opportunities by 2036 and raise the net incomes of young people by more than £2bn.

He said the main finding of the review was not a lack of ambition from young people but a lack of opportunities. “I have not met a single young person who wanted to be Neet [not in education, employment or training]. Not one. They want independence, they want to earn their own money and they want someone to give them a chance,” he said.

The Guardian revealed last month that ministers were working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping key disability benefits for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.

Charities are nervous about how the proposals will affect young people. The Joseph Rowntree Foundation said the proposals could significantly weaken the safety net for hundreds of thousands of young people with a disability or health condition, leaving many of those on universal credit living on a basic rate of support of just about £80 a week.

“Cutting someone’s income when they’re already struggling to afford food or the bus to college makes it harder for them to stay in education or find work,” said Iain Porter, the charity’s senior policy adviser.
More than 40 of the UK’s leading charities warned ministers earlier this year against imposing tougher benefit sanctions or cuts on disabled young people.

In their joint letter to Milburn and McFadden, they said cutting support or bringing in sanctions risked pushing thousands of vulnerable youngsters deeper into poverty and further away from employment.

Polling suggests that while the public favours cutting the welfare bill overall, they believe that tackling the root causes of joblessness instead of cutting benefits is the best way to do it. UK welfare spending has reached £333bn this year, with pensioners receiving roughly 55% of the budget, and young people including Neets – but not children – about 2.5%.
A government spokesperson said: “The Milburn and Timms reviews are due to be published shortly, and we will respond to their recommendations in full.

“We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work. But the prime minister has been clear that we need a wholesale change in the way we support young people to grow up in this country, where we invest in their success rather than paying for failure.”

articles.title: Microsoft outage hits hospitals, GPs, schools and police across UK
articles.summary: NHS suffering ‘serious’ and widespread disruption, while people are told of possible delays in receiving prescriptions
articles.byline: Ben Quinn, Aisha Down, Andrew Gregory and Jamie Grierson

blocks.text: Vital UK services including hospitals and police have been hit by a global Microsoft outage that left NHS staff resorting to paper records and fuelled concerns about an over-reliance on a small number of tech companies
A day of widespread disruption sent some sectors back to the 1990s, with court staff looking for fax machines and rail travellers being warned they may not be able to rely on digital tickets.

Schools, universities and businesses were also hit by the global outage affecting Microsoft’s 365 suite of products, which began late on Thursday evening and interrupted access to emails and calendars.

Hundreds of hospitals, GP surgeries and community health services were impacted as the NHS struggled to confirm appointment times, while pharmacists also warned of possible delays to prescriptions, and a union reported that ambulance services had suffered a “serious impact”.

The NHS.net Connect system – which more than one million NHS staff use for emails, meetings, calendars, file access and other tasks – is powered by Microsoft. The outage meant many could not log in, perform basic duties, or send and receive patient data needed for the delivery of healthcare.
Police forces across the UK told people to contact them by telephone if they needed to report crimes, instead of using online forms.

Tim Clement-Jones, a former chair of the House of Lords artificial intelligence select committee, said the widespread outages of vital government services were an “I-told-you-so moment” highlighting Britain’s dependence on a small number of US tech companies.

Lord Clement-Jones referenced a Guardian investigation in September that found senior police officials accepted the risk “US government insider” and foreign actors could compromise sensitive data as they moved key systems on to Microsoft.

“It is not a surprise that there is this dependency on a single ‘hyperscaler’, like Microsoft. I’ve got quite a lot of time for Microsoft as a business, but you don’t just put your eggs in one basket, and I’m afraid that’s what the government has been doing for some considerable period of time,” he said.

The UK government said it spent roughly £1.9bn on Microsoft software licences in 2025 and hundreds of millions more on Amazon and Google. There are no publicly available figures for how much key infrastructure is hosted on these platforms.

Documents previously obtained by the Guardian have indicated the police also believed thathosting their data on Microsoft’s platform put vital services at risk in case of an global outage – suggesting that first responders needed to consider having backup options in place.

In a warning echoed by others, Clement-Jones said the government had “just blindly procured”, adding: “They haven’t really seriously thought about the resilience required in our civil service – in our forms of email, communication, data storage, and so on. The easy thing to do is to buy the full suite from Microsoft.”

Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons science and technology committee, warned the outage highlighted the lack of resilience in the UK’s digital infrastructure and the dangers to security, economy and public services.

She referenced a report by her committee earlier this year which found that Britain was hugely dependent on a small number of US-based technology providers for its public services, preventing homegrown alternatives from developing.

“In its response, the government could not tell us how much it was spending on IT and digital or who it was spending it with. Without even knowing this, how can we protect against vendor lock-in or achieve the resilience and digital sovereignty the UK needs?” she said.
Downing Street said it was seeking to establish the “full picture” of Microsoft outages and urged the public to follow advice on “alternative ways to get in touch” where services were disrupted.

blocks.caption: National Rail warned that people may not be able to access tickets. Photograph: Posed by model; Oscar Wong/Getty Images

blocks.text: The problems began late on Thursday afternoon and users have been unable to access many of Microsoft’s most popular services. Thousands worldwide reported they were unable to send and receive emails through Outlook.

The Microsoft executive vice-president Charles Lamanna said the outages did not appear to be the result of a cyber-attack. On Friday morning, the firm said it was seeing “early signs of stabilisation”, later issuing an update that it was seeing email traffic being gradually restored.
NHS staff arriving at work on Friday morning reported being unable to access email, affecting their ability to deliver healthcare in hospitals and GP surgeries.

In some cases, staff said they were able to use their phones to access Microsoft Teams, which is heavily relied upon in the healthcare sector, but meetings were having to be cancelled across the board.

An NHS England spokesperson said: “Local NHS services are enacting longstanding measures to manage IT outages and ensure critical services and appointments can continue for patients today – including using other IT systems or paper records where possible.”

While travel disruption was limited and airports ran services as normal, National Rail warned that people may not be able to access tickets that have been emailed to them, advising customers to try to access them alternatively on websites or on apps.

The already backlogged court system was hit, with juries in some cases being sent home early or prisoners not being sent to court. At Minshull Street crown court in Manchester, Judge Maurice Greene said staff had been looking for a fax machine earlier in the morning.
“What we are learning is the dangers of our reliability on computer systems and platforms, and so on,” he told jurors before sending them home.

“Many institutions rely on Microsoft 365 as do the court and various institutions connected to the court, so there have all been sort of delays because of this. I would say sorry but it’s not my fault.”

“It may be Mr Gates’s fault but I don’t think he is going to come and apologise,” he added, referring to the cofounder of Microsoft, who officially resigned from Microsoft’s board of directors six years ago.

Businesses meanwhile braced for the impact of economic damage while the UK’s top financial regulators, the Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority, were hit by the Outlook outage, although a spokesperson for the bank said “all critical operations” were running normally.

However, the turmoil comes on the busiest day of the week for mortgage completions and there were also warnings that digital tickets for events could be affected, with Cheltenham racecourse urging visitors to arrive early.
Engineers from the government were working with Microsoft to assess the impact of the outage, according to a minister, while the Welsh government said it was putting contingency plans in place.
A Downing Street spokesperson said the prime minister was being kept updated on the situation, while individual departments would be able to rely on contingency plans where necessary.

They declined to say whether Downing Street itself had been affected, adding: “There are contingency measures in place at No 10, as there are with all government departments, to ensure that work can go on as usual.”
Asked about the effect specifically on the NHS, they said it appeared all clinical and operation systems were working effectively.

blocks.caption: Police said the outage was having an impact on people’s ability to report crimes using official websites. Photograph: Alphotographic/Getty Images

blocks.text: However, Britain’s minister for defence readiness and industry, Luke Pollard, said earlier in the morning that the outage demonstrated the need for “greater resilience” against technology failures.

Pollard told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “My appetite for disruption when it comes to using my phone is virtually zero. I imagine that’s the case for every one of your listeners, that people want it to work all the time, every time, and we’re seeing more disruption from those tech companies. That’s partly because we’ve become more dependent on technology.”

The government response was criticised by opposition MPs, with the Liberal Democrats describing it as a “national resilience failure” and calling for a minister to urgently come to brief MPs in parliament.
“No single provider should have such a major impact across the NHS, police and other frontline services,” said the Lib Dem Cabinet Office spokesperson Lisa Smart.
The cybersecurity minister, Liz Lloyd, said the outage had mainly affected back-office functions, such as messaging and email, and that 999 calls and NHS 111 services were unaffected.

“The government recognises this incident has been inconvenient and disruptive,” she said. “Affected departments and public sector organisations have plans in place for these events to mitigate potential impacts and continue their business operations. Throughout the day, we have seen limited reports of impact on frontline service delivery, and I encourage people to follow advice from the services they need on alternative ways to get in touch where email or web forms may be unavailable.

“We will review this incident and the lessons learned to inform our ongoing work to raise digital resilience across the UK, just as we are doing under the government cyber action plan and the cybersecurity and resilience bill.”

Police forces across the country said the Microsoft outage was having an impact on the ability to report crimes using official websites. “If your report is time-critical but not an emergency, please call 101. In an emergency, call 999,” said the Metropolitan police in London, as other forces issued similar advice.
School inspections in England were disrupted after Ofsted said it was unable to receive emails, as hundreds of schools, colleges and universities across the UK were affected.

The higher education sector was braced to be the hardest hit, with many UK universities relying on Outlook, OneDrive and other Microsoft services for administration and communications, although Teams appeared to be functioning for some online meetings.

articles.title: The dangers of revising Europe's security architecture
articles.summary: Experts warn against revising Europe's security framework because they say it would mean granting Moscow its longstanding wish of renegotiating postwar security on the continent.

image.caption: European leaders and diplomats met in Dublin to reaffirm their support for Ukraine as US-mediated peace talks gained momentum this week.Image: Virginia Mayo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: European leaders have so far found compromises in response to many of US President Donald Trump's demands.
But they were surprised to hear Trump say that he raised Europe's security framework with Russian officials.
"It's going to be a big agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House last week.
He said that deal might include all of Europe. But what he meant by "all of Europe" was not clear.
US envoy Jared Kushner also wrote that Europe and Russia had struggled to establish a sustainable security framework for more than 30 years.
Kushner said he was looking at a "broader" European architecture before he flew to meet with Russian and Ukrainian representatives in Abu Dhabi.

European diplomats immediately pushed back on Washington's approach to secure a peace deal in Ukraine because they feared that a peace settlement could restore Russia's sphere of influence and undermine NATO.

"We ​already have European security ​architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their ​respective roles. We ​must make sure Ukraine is integrated ‌into ⁠this architecture," said Kaja Kallas, the European Union's foreign policy chief.
The issue with revising Europe's postwar security framework
Russia made clear during talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week that they were keen to discuss a broader European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.

"Phrases about the European security architecture are certainly Russian talking points and not only talking points but, to a degree, part of a media propaganda effort that Russia makes to frame the war as it wishes to frame the war," said Michael Kimmage, a historian of the Cold War.
Russian leaders, including Vladimir Putin, have long alleged that the US and NATO repeatedly violated pledges they made in the early 1990s not to expand the alliance into the former Soviet bloc.
They have seen NATO's enlargement during this period as having put them in a humiliating position in which they could do very little.

At the same time, in the 1990s, the European project saw the birth of the European Union, the single market that ensured the free movement of goods and people across member states, the Schengen agreement for border-free travel, and the euro.
The core idea was to extend peace across the continent.
"Europe can mean so many things, but the European project was not designed for war. It was designed for peace," said Kimmage.
During this period, there were even suggestions of Russia becoming a NATO member.
But that relative period of stability changed after Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Russia wants to redraw all of this by force. And I think that that's fundamentally unacceptable to Europe with all the diversity and variations that you get within the European landscape on what's acceptable and not acceptable. I think the large-scale redrawing of borders by force is just not the European project," said Kimmage.
"So to the extent that the redrawing of borders by force is the lifeblood of Russian foreign policy, and I think that's a pretty easy case to make, Russia and Europe are at an impasse," he said.
What was to happen to Ukraine's security?

The Trump administration very quickly turned to making sure that "existing European security institutions" would be intact, with Jared Kushner having said late Thursday that the next round of negotiations would include "our European partners."
Kushner, along with Steve Witkoff, flew to Moscow to talk to Putin after talks in Abu Dhabi. Then they flew to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Kushner had earlier Thursday signaled some "really incredible" postwar plans for Ukraine, saying that it could not be concluded without Europeans at the table.

"We should not allow a diktat from Russia that would result in some kind of neutralization or significant reduction in the military forces of Ukraine going forward, because that would make Ukraine very, very vulnerable to future aggression and pressure coming from Russia," said Hiski Haukkala, the director of the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.
That would mean that Ukraine would also be completely dependent on the security guarantees that the US or Europeans are able and willing to provide.

"We are supporting Ukraine because we are supporting international law and the basic norms of decency and international security when it comes to European security architecture. And this is the vantage point from which we are operating," he said.
The European Union has repeatedly pointed to some of the basic treaties that Russia broke, including:

items: The UN Charter
The Helsinki Act of 1975, which established the ten core principles of European security, including the non-use of force or threat against territorial integrity.
The Charter of Paris for a New Europe that built on Helsinki commitments
The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), which was one of the few multilateral security forums where the West and Russia engaged.
The Budapest Memorandum of 1994 in which Russia, the US and the UK provided security assurances to Ukraine and others in exchange for them giving up their nuclear weapons.

blocks.text: "Russia walked away from these principles and smashed them to pieces in the process. And they are not interested in reinstating the previous security architecture order. They want something different in its stead. And as long as this is not on the table, the Russian form of negotiation is to wage war. War is a form of bargaining," Haukkala said.
"And they are signaling strategic intent to change the makeup of European security, to subdue Ukraine and to change the very essence of European security," he added.

blocks.caption: US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Volodymyr Zelenskyy after having met Vladimir Putin in Moscow.Image: Peter Morrison/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What is the way forward?
Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for European Affairs in the George W. Bush administration, said Russia is very good at sticking to its demands.
He said Russians know how to negotiate and "right now, they are not negotiating," referring to talks in Abu Dhabi.
Some experts said there was no possibility of having a new security architecture with the Russians at this point because there was no trust or common vision to align with Russia at the moment.
Others like Balazs Jarabik, an expert on post-Soviet politics, said that Russia was part of the European security architecture whether Europeans liked it or not.

"And the question is whether it's included as our enemy. Obviously, Russia is not going to be a partner, right? We have to find a modus operandi to reduce the risk of a horizontal escalation and potentially a bigger European war, even a bigger one than what we have now."

A host of European leaders on Friday rejected the Russian demands to discuss Europe's security framework as well, with a spokesperson for the German government saying that Berlin was looking to host a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" to secure funding for Ukraine's defense and reach a unified position regarding future peace talks.
Can Germany make Europe pay more for Ukraine?

articles.title: Kindergarten Cop child actor Christian Cousins dead at 43
articles.summary: Former child actor Christian Cousins, who shared the role of Dominic Palmieri in Kindergarten Cop with his twin brother, Joey, has died at 43. His half-brother, Jonas Roeser, announced the news on…

image.caption: Former child actor Christian Cousins, pictured in August 2017, has died at 43, his brother announced in an Instagram post. (Christian Cousins/Facebook)

blocks.text: Entertainment

Former child actor Christian Cousins, who shared the role of Dominic Palmieri in Kindergarten Cop with his twin brother, Joey, has died at 43. His half-brother, Jonas Roeser, announced the news on Instagram, writing Cousins had been seriously ill with liver disease.
His brother, Jonas Roeser, announced his death in an Instagram post last month
Christian Cousins, the former child actor who shared the role of Dominic Palmieri in Kindergarten Cop with his twin brother, Joey, has died at 43.

Cousins's brother Jonas Roeser announced his death in an Instagram post last month. Roeser said Cousins had been "very sick with liver disease." The Oct. 22 post did not give a cause of death beyond that information or specify the date he died.
"It’s hard to share that my brother, Christian Cousins, has passed away," Roeser wrote.

Roeser said that he and the twins were siblings through their biological father, but grew up in different states — Christian and Joseph in California, and Jonas in Washington. He noted that he did not get to know them until he was in college. Before then, he watched their work on television and in the movies.
"Those roles are only a small part of how I’ll remember Christian," Roeser wrote. "He was a character, full of passion and energy, with big stories and even bigger dreams."

Cousins and his twin brother played Dominic Palmieri in the 1990 comedy Kindergarten Cop, starring Arnold Schwarzenegger as a police detective who goes undercover as a kindergarten teacher. The brothers shared the role, appearing alongside Schwarzenegger and Penelope Ann Miller.
Years later, during a 30th anniversary reunion, Schwarzenegger noted that the children "made this movie" and that their performances were what made the film so endearing to audiences.
Penelope Ann Miller, left, and Arnold Schwarzenegger, right, in Kindergarten Cop. (Universal Pictures)

Beyond his cinematic turn in Kindergarten Cop, Cousins was a familiar face on television in the late 1980s and early 1990s. He and Joseph appeared in nearly 60 episodes of the prime-time soap opera Knots Landing, portraying Bobby Gibson Ewing between 1987 and 1992. The twins also appeared in several other projects, including Critters 3 (1991), Intruders (1992) and Twin Sitters (1994), before retiring from acting in 1995.
In his tribute, Roeser expressed a sense of peace knowing that his brother is no longer suffering.
"It brings me comfort to believe he is now in heaven with his mother, free from the pain he was carrying," he wrote. "Rest easy, Christian. I hope your soul is at rest and that you’ve found peace."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Christine Pagulayan is a Toronto-based producer and writer with CBC News, currently with the Entertainment unit. She has worked in various roles at CBC News Network and The National. She has also worked as a multiplatform reporter in Toronto, Winnipeg, Halifax and Moncton. You can reach her at christine.pagulayan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Home sales hit 16-year low in October amid soaring mortgage rates
articles.summary:
Sales of built units fell to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, with mortgage rates at nearly three-year high

US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were…

blocks.text: US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were driven away by high mortgage rates and rising inflation, according to new data released on Wednesday.

Sales of already built units dropped to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, the National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported. The median existing-home sales price increased slightly to $416,700. Declines in sales were seen in the midwest, south and west, though sales in the north-east held steady.

Mortgage rates had been steadily declining in 2024 and 2025, with the 30-year rate falling below 6% for the first time in February 2026. But increasing inflation and higher interest rates amid the Iran war have pushed rates back up to a nearly three-year high.

The 30-year mortgage rate, which is the most commonly used rate in home loans, is now hovering at about 7.18%, not far from its 2023 high of 7.79%. During the pandemic, average mortgage rates were just above 3%.

“Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Lawrence Yun, chief economist at the NAR. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”

Pending home sales, or the number of contracts that have been signed before closing, reached its lowest levels in the NAR’s history in September, the same month that the 30-year mortgage rate topped 7% for the first time in nearly two years.

Mortgage rates have been directly affected by interest rate changes by the US Federal Reserve, which in September hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023. Rates currently sit at a range of 3.75% to 4%.
The central bank is poised to raise rates again next month to combat heightened inflation, which went up more than expected in October.
after newsletter promotion

Affordability and cost-of-living concerns played an outsized role in the midterm elections that gave Democrats control of Congress next year. According to the latest census data, growth in median rent across the US outpaced inflation. The home-ownership rate in the US has stagnated since 2021, according to the same data.

“I don’t think this is a new normal for home sales,” said Danielle Hale, chief economist at Realtor.com. “Instead, it reflects a perfect storm of an abrupt shift in the financial environment and large uncertainties in the pre-election period for both policy and the economy just as the housing market usually slows for the season.”

articles.title: Microsoft outage shakes up companies, schools and local governments across US
articles.summary: Local officials warn some services remain unavailable even as Outlook starts to resume normal operations after outage

blocks.text: The Microsoft Outlook outage has shaken up companies and local governments across the US that use its suite of email, calendar, video conferencing and cloud storage systems.

Even as Outlook started to resume normal operations Friday morning, local leaders from across the country, including in Miami, Maryland and Los Angeles, warned residents that certain staff or services were still unavailable due to the outage that started around 1pm ET on Thursday.
In Colorado, one local detention facility in Arapahoe county said that they were unable to take online bond payments to release detainees because of the outage.
“Until Outlook email is restored, anyone needing to post bond for immediate release must do so in person at the jail,” the office said in a social media statement.
The Los Angeles county sheriff’s department also warned that it was experiencing disruptions in its email and other communications platforms.
Emergency management services in Fredericksburg and Gillespie county in Texas said they were unable to receive emails and encouraged residents and partners to call instead.

Around Maryland, the Washington suburban sanitary commission, which provides safe drinking water and sewer treatment to parts of Maryland, said that its technicians may be delayed due to the outage, and some customers may have trouble making their water bill payments.

In Washington DC, congressional staffers continued to lament the outage’s impact during the lame duck session of Congress. Some told Politico that the disruptions were particularly disruptive as their offices were in the middle of negotiating pending legislation before the end of the year and planning for the next Congress.
“Shall we start conducting all official business via DM?” wrote Sharon Eliza Nichols, the director of communications for congresswoman Eleanor Holmes Norton of Washington DC.

Some school districts in Richmond, Virginia, and Port Washington, New York, also told parents on Friday morning that they were experiencing outages, and asked them to reach out by phone or through other online educational platforms to reach their child’s school, while the Albany school district said that it had restored its services.

The Colorado School of Mines encouraged “faculty to be flexible with assignment deadlines and understanding of students who cannot complete assignments due to unavailability of Microsoft tools”, though many of its systems were on unaffected platforms such as Google Workspace and Canvas.

Claude, whose developer, Anthropic, is gearing up for its upcoming stock market debut with a valuation of up to $1.4tn, also said that it was starting to see signs of recovery from the Microsoft outages, but warned that some users may still receive errors. OpenAI also said it was still investigating issues with “Microsoft connectors” that were degrading performance.
“We’re investigating an issue with Microsoft connectors where new connections may be broken and tools are not working as expected. We’ll share an update when we know more,” the company said.
On Wall Street, Workhorse Group, an industrial manufacturer, rescheduled its Q3 earnings call that was scheduled for Thursday afternoon because of the outage.
In a social media post, Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said late Thursday that “there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity”.

On Friday morning, Microsoft noted “improvements in service availability” but noted that “some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as a recovery continues”.

articles.title: Former Hamas bodyguard convicted of Birmingham knife crime also wanted in Germany
articles.summary:
Mohammed Alfatih rearrested over alleged plot to target Israelis in Europe while detained for attack on bailiff

A former Hamas bodyguard convicted of knife crime in the UK is wanted in…

blocks.text: A former Hamas bodyguard convicted of knife crime in the UK is wanted in Germany for allegedly plotting to murder Jewish people.
Details of the plot can now be reported after Mohammed Alfatih, also known as Mohammed Naim, was found guilty on Friday of a knife attack on a bailiff outside his home in Birmingham.
The 40-year-old was found guilty by a majority verdict of unlawful wounding, possession of two knives and criminal damage. He was cleared of the more serious charge of wounding with intent.
He was under surveillance by a counter-terrorism unit when he attacked the bailiff last year.
Alfatih, the son of a senior Hamas official, could not be named during his trial because of reporting restrictions.
He had been photographed working for a former leader of Hamas before being granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020.
While detained for the attack on the bailiff in Birmingham, he was rearrested after authorities in Germany said he had been part of an alleged plot to attack Israeli targets in central Europe.
Alfatih, who was born in Germany, is expected to be extradited to the country after he has served his sentence in the UK, with his connection to Hamas stated in the German extradition request.

German prosecutors charged seven suspected Hamas members in September over an alleged plot to target Jews or Israelis in Germany or Austria around the second anniversary of the 7 October attack on Israel.

They said “Mohammed A” played a prominent role in transporting and storing weapons but was being prosecuted separately after UK authorities arrested him in London and noted he had not yet been returned to Germany.
German authorities said he was connected to Hamas’s leadership and was said to have produced a video in advance to take responsibility for the attack on its behalf.
The attack was disrupted by Germany’s domestic intelligence service after a tipoff from the Mossad, Israel’s secret service.
During a two-week trial at Birmingham crown court, the jury was shown video footage of Alfatih lashing out with a knife at the broken window of a van on 14 October last year.
The bailiff, Kevin Bucknall, was left with cuts to his head and required hospital treatment. The defendant pleaded not guilty on the grounds of self-defence.
The jurors, who convicted Alfatih after being shown film footage of him brandishing two large kitchen knives outside his home in Kings Heath, Birmingham, were not told of his links to Hamas.
They were also not told Alfatih was under surveillance by a counter-terrorism unit after being released on bail on suspicion of a terror offence days before the bailiff was attacked.
A government source said: “This is a staggering example of the loss of border control under the last Conservative government, who granted his asylum claim and gave him citizenship.
“This Labour government has just introduced reforms that ensure those who gain citizenship must first show they are a good citizen and have contributed to this country.”

articles.title: SpaceX to attempt to catch its first Starship on land in 15th flight
articles.summary: SpaceX's latest Starship flight planned for Friday will include its first attempt to catch the spacecraft at its Texas launch site, rather than discarding it in ‌the ocean — a key test of Elon Musk's…

image.caption: Visitors pose in front of Starship 42, atop the Super Heavy v3 Booster 22, as it's poised for its 15th test flight from the SpaceX launch complex in Starbase, Texas, on Friday. SpaceX plans to return and capture the booster and Starship after the launch. (Reuters/Joe Skipper)

blocks.text: Science·New

SpaceX's latest Starship flight planned for Friday will include its first attempt to catch the spacecraft at its Texas launch site, rather than discarding it in ‌the ocean — a key test of Elon Musk's bid to make a fully reusable rocket system.
NASA and SpaceX expect Starship ​to land humans on the moon by 2028

The 124-metre-tall Starship rocket is scheduled to launch at 5:45 p.m. ET from SpaceX's Starbase launch facilities in South Texas for its 15th flight since 2023 and the second to carry a batch of operational Starlink satellites. That makes the mission both a revenue-generating endeavour for ​its satellite connectivity business and a high-stakes test for a rocket still in development.

SpaceX, ​as of Friday morning, had not received a launch licence from the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The FAA, which has typically issued licences a day prior to past Starship launches, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Musk's ​space and AI colossus views the next-generation Starship rocket as crucial to expanding its Starlink network with more satellites ⁠and, in the future, deploying a ⁠vast swarm of AI data-processing satellites called Starmind, as the company increasingly positions ‌itself as an infrastructure giant.

SpaceX last launched Starship in September, taking the rocket and its satellites to orbit for the first time despite some engines shutting down mid-flight. That mission, planned to last 10 hours, ended after roughly three hours with an intact splashdown in the Pacific Ocean.
SpaceX catches Starship rocket booster intact

For Friday's mission, the company expects to return to Texas both Starship's Super Heavy booster and ⁠the Starship upper stage it launches to space. The upper stage — the top half of the rocket that serves as the spacecraft — will return some 22 hours after launch. SpaceX has said it would be a "breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket" if all goes as planned.
Making way for Starship

SpaceX has returned the 71-metre-tall Super Heavy booster three times to its launchpad after sending Starship to space, falling back vertically into large mechanical arms fixed to its launch tower some 10 minutes after launch. The last such "tower catch" was in March 2025.

For the 15th mission, SpaceX will need to move the Super Heavy booster off the launchpad to make way for Starship, which is ​expected to fall from space after completing 14 orbits around Earth. That sets up the debut Starship catch to occur around 3:45 p.m. ET on Saturday.

items: Starlink satellites create light pollution and disrupt radio frequencies. And it's getting worse
SpaceX wants to launch a million satellites. Here's how that could impact the atmosphere and the night sky

blocks.text: Musk has said he expects to ⁠enter a weekly cadence of Starship launches by the first half of 2027, while SpaceX has said it could begin launching Starship from a ⁠new Florida launchpad by the end of 2026.

NASA has helped fund Starship's development with roughly $3.2 billion US delivered to SpaceX since selecting the ⁠rocket in 2021 ⁠to serve as a moon lander for its ​astronauts under the multibillion-dollar Artemis moon program. SpaceX has put at least $15 billion US of its own funds into the rocket's development.
Video shows fiery, falling debris after SpaceX rocket breaks up
NASA and SpaceX expect Starship ​to land humans on the moon by 2028, ⁠though several major testing milestones remain that analysts and industry engineers believe will push that timeline back.
Those milestones include demonstrating complex fuel transfers between Starship "tanker" rockets in orbit — a key process that will enable Starship to travel beyond Earth's orbit to the moon.

Jeff Bezos's Blue Origin is also developing a moon lander, Blue Moon, for NASA under the Artemis program. Blue Moon is poised to join Starship and another spacecraft, NASA's Orion capsule, in Earth's orbit next year for ⁠Artemis III, a docking test mission before NASA's ‌planned moon landing missions begin with Artemis IV.
