articles.title: SWS: Marcos administration's net satisfaction rating drops to -4 in September 2026
articles.summary: Filipino adults gave the national government a net satisfaction rating of -4 in September 2026, down from the previous survey, according to results released by the Social Weather Stations (SWS) on…

blocks.text: Filipino adults gave the national government a net satisfaction rating of -4 in September 2026, down from the previous survey, according to results released by the Social Weather Stations (SWS) on Friday.

Although SWS classified the -4 rating as “neutral,” it represented a five-point decline from the +1 recorded in June 2026, making it the second-lowest net satisfaction rating of President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr.’s administration. The latest survey was conducted from September 21 to 27, 2026.
In March 2026, the Marcos administration recorded its lowest net satisfaction rating at "poor" -13.

“Thirty-eight percent of adult Filipinos were satisfied, 18% were neither satisfied nor dissatisfied, and 42% were dissatisfied with the general performance of the current National Administration, for a net satisfaction rating of -4,” SWS said.
Performance subjects
In its Governance Report Card, SWS assessed the national administration's performance across various areas, with ratings ranging from “very good” to “bad.”

“The National Administration’s net satisfaction rating was very good on providing the youth with basic education in public elementary and high schools (+61) and improving the quality of children’s education (+50),” the survey said.

“It was good on helping the poor (+42, correctly rounded), implementing housing programs for the poor (+40), creating policies that will generate job opportunities (+40), helping victims of disasters (+36, correctly rounded), and developing science and technology (+30, correctly rounded),” it added.
The national government received “moderate” ratings for ensuring food safety, providing an efficient transportation system, and defending Philippine sovereignty in the West Philippine Sea.
Meanwhile, it received a “poor” rating for generating solutions to rising oil prices and a “bad” rating for eradicating graft and corruption in government and fighting inflation.
SWS said net satisfaction ratings declined across all 19 performance subjects compared with the previous survey.

“Compared to November 2025, when they were last surveyed, net satisfaction fell by 23 points for being prepared for strong typhoons, from moderate +28 to neutral +5, and by 14 points for helping victims of disasters, from very good +50 to good +36,” it added.
Regional ratings
The administration recorded its highest net satisfaction rating in Balance Luzon at neutral +7, followed by the Visayas at neutral -2, Mindanao at poor -17, and Metro Manila at poor -21.

"Compared to June 2026, net satisfaction with the National Administration fell by 10 points in Metro Manila, from poor -11 to poor -21. It fell by 7 points in the Visayas, from neutral +5 to neutral -2, and by 6 points in Balance Luzon, from moderate +13 to neutral +7. It stayed at poor -17 in Mindanao," SWS said.

The administration also recorded declines in net satisfaction ratings among 18- to 24-year-olds (+13 to -13), college graduates (-10 to -25), those with some senior high school through some college (+4 to -16), men (-3 to -6), and women (+6 to -1).

The net satisfaction rating improved but remained poor among those aged 35 to 44, rising by four points from -15 to -11. Meanwhile, it remained moderate among adults aged 55 and above, edging up by one point from +17 to +18.

The survey was conducted through face-to-face interviews with 1,500 adults aged 18 and above nationwide: 600 in Balance Luzon (or Luzon outside Metro Manila) and 300 each in Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao.
The sampling error margins were ±3 percentage points for national figures, ±4 points for Balance Luzon, and ±6 points each for Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Democratic Senate leader Schumer set to face leadership challenge
articles.summary: Maryland Senator Van Hollen says "new leadership" is needed for Democrats following the party's recent midterm successes.

blocks.text: US Senator Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge to his position as US Senate majority leader from his fellow Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, as the party prepares to take control of Congress after sweeping the midterm elections.
Van Hollen, 67, said in a post on X on Thursday that Americans voted for change earlier this month and "to deliver, we need new leadership".
Schumer, 75, has led Democrats in the chamber since 2017, serving as both majority and minority leader. He was first elected to the Senate in 1999.
Following the midterms earlier this month, his position has come under pressure by some left-wing Democrats who see him as too moderate and part of the party establishment.
Responding to the challenge, Schumer, who represents New York, said he welcomes "any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead".
He added that he is "proud of what we've accomplished together" in the midterms, and he has "the votes to continue as Democratic leader".

The vote on Senate leader will be held behind closed doors in early December and the winner will assume the role on 4 January, when Democrats take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives after their midterms successes.
The move by Van Hollen, who represents Maryland, marks the most significant step by a high-profile Democrat to challenge the party's existing leadership following last week's midterms victory.
Announcing his plans to run on X, he wrote that Americans had called on the party to "unrig an economy rigged against working people".
In recent years, Van Hollen has taken positions popular with those on the left of his party.
In 2024, he supported restricting weapons shipments to Israel and criticised the Biden administration over its role in the war in Gaza.
In an interview with MS NOW, Van Hollen - who has served in the Senate for nearly a decade - acknowledged that he is an "underdog" but added that he believes the race is "very much in flux".
Independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed have both publicly come out in support of Van Hollen - while others have also called for new leadership.
In a post on X, Sanders said he believes Van Hollen "will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families".
El-Sayed said the challenger would bring "bold leadership" and lead with both "courage and experience".
Others Democrats have publicly backed Schumer.
Senator Jacky Rosen of Nevada said: "He has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment".
Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said: "You will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position."

articles.title: German spies handed new powers to tackle 'hybrid threats' from abroad
articles.summary: German reforms mean foreign and domestic intelligence services will have greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage.

blocks.text: Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's parliament, the Bundestag, approved a major overhaul of its legislation.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who championed the bill, has called it a "reform of the century", necessary because of the increasing threats from foreign powers.
But the Left Party's security spokeswoman, Clara Bünger, said Dobrindt was creating a new German secret police.
The legislation gives numerous new powers to Germany's BND federal intelligence service, and its BfV domestic service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.
In the Bundestag, 309 MPs voted in favour of the new law on intelligence services, while 190 voted against and 71 abstained.
For historical reasons, German intelligence has mainly focused on gathering information rather than acting on it.
In future, German spies working for the BND, which is responsible for foreign intelligence, will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, including sabotage.
This could include paralysing the servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks, or even disrupting supply chains for weapons.

Agents for the domestic intelligence service, the BfV, will no longer to be limited to gathering information. For the first time they will be able to take protective action against property and IT systems, if specific threats are identified.

That means they will be allowed to dismantle or break explosives or weapons, divert or block data flows during cyber-attacks, delete or falsify data stored for malicious purposes, and plant false information on those involved.
Under certain conditions, BfV agents will also be permitted to enter homes covertly. However, the measure must always be authorised in advance.

They will also be given wider powers of digital surveillance, including monitoring encrypted telecommunications and carrying out online searches. They will also be allowed to use AI-supported data analysis and biometric image matching on the internet.
The government says the reform is needed because of an increase in foreign espionage, particularly from Russia, China and Iran.
"We are the target of hybrid threats," said Dobrindt. "Germany is a theatre of operations for terrorism, extremism and foreign powers."
In August, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig Airport, close to Ukrainian cargo planes. However, it failed to explode as the bomb's detonator was apparently faulty.
German authorities say Russia was behind the attack.
The new law has been bitterly criticised by some opposition politicians, even though Dobrindt has said it is "madness" to think it means that Germany is creating a new secret police.
And Clara Bünger from the Left Party told public broadcaster ARD that the new law was "a monster… summoning ghosts that we will probably never be able to get rid of".
The separation between the police and the secret service, she warned, was "being eroded" - and Bünger said that had been a lesson learned from the Nazi era.
"This means the secret service is being granted executive powers and will not only be allowed to act pre-emptively, but will also be granted police powers."

However, Sonja Eichwede of the centre-left SPD, which is part of Germany's governing coalition, said the reforms would make a significant contribution to ensuring the country's democracy was "robust and resilient".

articles.title: Nvidia scandal fallout widens as Trump's treasury secretary blames cabinet colleague
articles.summary: Scott Bessent suggests Howard Lutnick’s commerce department failed to ban exports of Nvidia's chips to a firm thought to have links with China.

blocks.text: How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?
ByRachel Clun
Business ReporterReporting fromNew York

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed the Commerce Department, run by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec Nvidia chips, as the fallout from the scandal widens.
Jensen Huang left Nvidia after revelations he had an affair with a former Megaspeed executive who was also allegedly a Chinese spy. The firm had been buying advanced chips from Nvidia.

Megaspeed had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it had been smuggling chips into China, reports said, but it is not on a list of firms that US companies are prevented from working with.
Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".
"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.
There is growing pressure on Lutnick from both sides of politics to explain his department's actions.
He has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to keep all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images
Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China.

"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.

Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.

There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included.
However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.
"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme, external.

"The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?
"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."
Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
The Commerce Secretary has been summoned to appear before the committee in December.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman, Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X.

Democrats on key congressional committees have also asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E. Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations over the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.
According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into America for inspection.

A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security.
"Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What caused the Microsoft outage?
articles.summary: Thousands of users worldwide were affected by a widespread Microsoft outage, with several institutions in the Philippines also reporting disruptions. Around 74 countries were affected by the outage,…

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 11:37pm
Thousands of users worldwide were affected by a widespread Microsoft outage, with several institutions in the Philippines also reporting disruptions.
Around 74 countries were affected by the outage, according to Down Detector.

In a report from GMA News Feed, Microsoft first announced the outage on X at 11:40 p.m. on November 12, Philippine time. The report said that they were investigating reported issues in Microsoft Teams in parts of North America.
Later, Microsoft said that it received reports of difficulty in accessing cloud-based messaging Exchange Online.
Down Detector said it has received 97,000 reports of difficulty accessing Microsoft Outlook in the US, as of 3:00 a.m. in the Philippines, November 13.
Meanwhile, there were 38,000 reports of issues with Microsoft 365, while 4,500 users reported problems with Microsoft Teams.
Down Detector said it received reports from the United Kingdom, India and New Zealand. Australia also said that its Federal Police at the Security Intelligence Organization was affected.
OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, was also affected. They said that they were probing issues with Microsoft connectors, which led to some of their tools malfunctioning.
In the Philippines, the Supreme Court issued an advisory on November 13 that its judiciary platform was affected. Because of this, some transactions may be delayed.

“The Supreme Court informs the public that the ongoing worldwide Microsoft 365 service outage has affected the Philippine Judiciary 365 (PJ365), including Microsoft Outlook. During this period, responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed,” the high court said.
Microsoft said that it was not increased traffic that caused this mass outage. The firm attributed the outage to some servers being unavailable, which affected its remaining infrastructure.

As of 4:14 a.m. in the Philippines, Microsoft said that based on their investigation, another possible reason for the unavailable servers was due to one “specific component” that focuses on the health of the servers.

“Our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health. We've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being impacted while we work to return the affected servers to service,” the tech giant said.
As of 2:12 p.m. in the Philippines, Microsoft said that it was continuously working to fix its frontend servers and restore its service infrastructure to a healthy state.—Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Why does El Salvador's Bukele have troops in Haiti?
articles.summary: Haiti's Prime Minister congratulating El Salvador's President for a gang crackdown in Haiti has shone a light on the relationship between the two countries. What's going on, and where does the US…

image.caption: Salvadorean soldiers have become a familiar site in Port-au-Prince, HaitiImage: Patrice Noel/REUTERS

blocks.text: Haiti has been engulfed in crisis since 2018, with protests, a presidential assassination and widespread gang violence bringing the country to its knees.

But earlier this week, Haiti's Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime hailed a major win in the battle against the violence, thanks to "the commitment of the Salvadorean forces in the fight against gangs."

El Salvador's President, Nayib Bukele had earlier said a joint task force between the countries had "destroyed" what he called "the house of Lanmo San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters." He also tweeted out an as-yet unverified video of helicopters firing on a sprawling property.
Why are troops from El Salvador in Haiti?
A number of Salvadoran troops have been stationed in Haiti, nearly 2,000 kilometers from their homeland, since the beginning of 2025, mostly in an attempt to curb gang influence.
Last month, Bukele dispatched more than 2,000 troops and special forces to Haiti, ostensibly to rescue four Salvadorans who were ambushed on October 18 and have not yet been found.
How the West messed with Haiti

Writing on social media platform X, Fils-Aime thanked the Salvadorean military for helping "the fight against gangs." The two nations are, he added, working alongside the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), in an attempt to "regain control of the territory and restore state authority."
The GSF has been operating in Haiti since 2016. But there are doubts to the legitimacy of El Salvador's presence.

"Where the lines are and where the coordination begins and ends between a bunch of distinct entities and security forces is a huge concern about how this actually plays out, and El Salvador are trying to frame it as their choice, their action," Jake Johnston, a Haiti expert and director of international research at the Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR) in Washington, told non-profit news agency The New Humanitarian this week.
What is the current situation in Haiti?

A UN report about Haiti released on Thursday described "bloody turf wars, sexual violence and other horrors, noting that serious violations and abuses continue to be committed across the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area and in the Artibonite and South-East departments."

It further found that between July and September 2026, at least 1,167 people were killed and 459 injured, with more than half of that violence stemming from "ground or aerial operations carried out by security forces against gangs, sometimes with the support of a private military company using drones."

blocks.caption: Salvadoran troops in armored vehicles patrol the streets of HaitiImage: Fildor Pq Egeder/REUTERS

blocks.text: For many observers, this chaos is a major part of the appeal for Bukele, who appears to wish to export his mano dura (iron fist) policy on to foreign soil. The policy saw gang members jailed on a huge scale and a significant drop in the murder rate of a country once notorious for homicide. But Romain Le Cour Grandmaison, a Haiti expert from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, told DW earlier this month that Haiti's gang problem is more entrenched. He says using the same tactics as in El Salvador may not have the same result.

"Haiti does not currently have the conditions to replicate the Salvadoran model: Its prisons were emptied in 2024, its justice system is largely paralyzed and criminal groups resemble militias more than gangs, with territory, taxes, weapons of war and political networks that protect them," Le Cour Grandmaison said.
Does El Salvador have US support?

Despite El Salvador being on Donald Trump's list of "shithole countries" that the US president disparaged in 2018 in notorious remarks which he later partially denied, relations between the US and El Salvador have improved markedly during Trump's second term.

blocks.caption: Nayib Bukele has tried to position himself as an ally to Donald Trump Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The number of migrants deported to El Salvador from the US rose by 98% at the start of 2026 and Le Cour Grandmaison said the US plays "a central, albeit very discreet, role in public life" in El Salvador.

Bukele's move to position himself as an ally of Trump has seen the US president offer him a level of endorsement and autonomy to do what Bukele deems necessary to protect El Salvador's security and that of its troops.
"He said that he has a big problem with Haiti. I said: 'Look, you're running your country. You have to do what you have to do,'" Trump said in November.

articles.title: 15 United Conservative constituency presidents won't sign agreement to publicly back Alberta referendum result
articles.summary: Presidents of 15 United Conservative Party constituency associations say they won’t sign a revised code of conduct requiring them to publicly respect and abide by the result of a provincial…

image.caption: The United Conservative Party board is facing pushback from some constituency presidents on a requirement to publicly endorse the result of a national unity referendum, as party members prepare for their annual general meeting in Calgary at the end of November. (Bob Grieve/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New

Presidents of 15 United Conservative Party constituency associations say they won’t sign a revised code of conduct requiring them to publicly respect and abide by the result of a provincial referendum on national unity.
Presidents say party's board doesn't have authority to issue the demand

In a letter obtained by CBC News, the locally elected constituency board presidents say they disagree the party has the authority to change the code of conduct without members voting on the change. Four of the people listed on the letter told CBC News the letter was authentic.

The presidents, who are from constituencies in Edmonton, Calgary and beyond, also say such a demand doesn’t belong in a code of conduct, and contradicts an existing code provision that protects their freedom of expression.

“I believe they've overstepped their boundaries, and really I wanted it just to go away,” said Robert Such, president of the UCP constituency association in Calgary-Klein, whose name is on the letter.

In an interview on Thursday, Such said he has a strong sense of western alienation and is glad Alberta held an October referendum on whether to hold a second, binding referendum on the province pursuing independence from Canada.
“I'm happy it's done,” he said. “Let's move on to bigger things. Some people just can't stop litigating this.”

items: Official results of Alberta referendum released

blocks.text: Days after three-quarters of voters who cast ballots in the Oct. 19 referendum indicated they wanted Alberta to remain in Canada, Premier Danielle Smith said in a video message to fellow UCP members that anyone who publicly represents the party must abide by Alberta voters’ federalist wishes.
Smith said that would include any candidates running for the party, UCP board members and the presidents of constituency associations in the province’s 87 ridings.

items: Alberta premier says UCP must be pro-Canada, separatists can 'join a different party'
UCP board candidates must sign declaration to abide by Alberta's vote to stay in Canada

blocks.text: Earlier this week, the party’s executive director sent all constituency association presidents a new non-disclosure agreement and code of conduct document to sign by Friday.

The UCP did not answer CBC News' questions by publication time about what the potential consequences would be for any constituency association president who refused to sign the document. Earlier this week, UCP spokesman Dave Prisco told CBC in an emailed statement the party intends to "honour" the referendum's outcome.
Demand conflicts with UCP’s ethos: political scientist
Such said he thinks there’s little the party can do, which is why he felt comfortable declining. If the party cancels memberships in response, “We’re just electing the NDP,” he said.

Such said he does not think the party is rife with members who will continue the push for independence from Canada. He said his Calgary constituency association is more concerned with finding a high-quality candidate that appeals to urban, federalist voters for Oct. 18, 2027, the fixed election date.
University of Calgary political science Prof. Lisa Young said she believes the party board’s requirement for local leaders to back the referendum result conflicts with the UCP’s culture.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks to party faithful at the United Conservative Party annual general meeting in Calgary, Saturday, Nov. 4, 2023. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)
“It’s a party that very much values the idea of bottom-up, grassroots influence on government, on the party leader,” she said in an interview.

To introduce such a rule, the party could ask members to vote on a motion at its upcoming annual general meeting in Calgary, starting Nov. 27, Young said. However, she noted leaders may be afraid members won’t support it.
She said it’s possible the annual general meeting will be a “fractious event” instead of the type of cohesive gathering one might expect before a provincial election.

“I think you're going to see a lot of mobilization from the floor trying to push back against this sort of new top-down set of rules from the party leadership,” Young said. “Who will win coming out of a contest like that?”
Even if an attempt at forcing a unity message from party representatives leads members to leave the party — or be forced out — Young doesn’t think it’ll be a huge setback.

items: Alberta separatist Jeff Rath kicked out of governing United Conservative Party

blocks.text: Elections Alberta figures show the UCP has so far raised $5.2 million in donations for the first three quarters of 2026, and this total may not include all constituency level contributions.
The Opposition Alberta NDP has reported nearly $3.6 million in contributions during the same period.
Young said she believes it's a bigger risk if a contingent of UCP members defect to another political party organized enough to garner votes, which could then split right-leaning voters.

“Smith is going to face a difficult election coming up,” Young said. “She's got to be thinking about that, because she's not doing particularly well in the polls while she's also fighting on another front with her own party.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Janet French covers the Alberta Legislature for CBC Edmonton. She previously spent 15 years working at newspapers, including the Edmonton Journal and Saskatoon StarPhoenix. You can reach her at janet.french@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Iran targeted US radar system in Bahrain
articles.summary: Iran claimed it struck US radar systems in Bahrain, while the US said it had intercepted the attacks. Clashes continue in the Strait of Hormuz, as the war remains in a state of de-escalation.

image.caption: The Strait of Hormuz is a vital chokepoint for oil and gas transport [FILE: October 12, 2026]Image: REUTERS

blocks.text: Iran said its forces hit a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday. However, the US military denied the claims and said it shot down two Iranian attack drones.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) initially said in a statement that its air force targeted and destroyed the radar on the island of Bahrain.
They claimed this was a retaliatory attack in response to an US attack on a telecommunications tower in the Iranian county of Sirik, on the shores of the Strait of Hormuz.
Several hours later, the US military's Central Command, denied the IRGC's claim that the radar was destroyed and said it stopped two "one-way attack drones" targeting Bahrain by the militant group.
It reported no casualties or damage.
How serious are Iran's new threats of retaliation?
Where does the Iran war stand?
Iran war, started by the US and Israeli strikes on February 28, is currently undergoing a de-escalation as main issues remain unresolved.
Both US and Israel are holding off major attacks as they held elections over the last weeks.

On the other hand, Tehran has continued seeking to control the Strait of Hormuz, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, while continuing to attack ships it considers unauthorized users of the waterway.
Iran conflict: Could a new phase of the war be imminent?
The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait in the area where reports of burning ships came through.
Before the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump said on October, "We may do another little Epic Fury," referring to US-Israeli strikes, without giving any timeframe.
Trump is expected to meet Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at an APEC leaders' summit in China next week and discuss ending the ​war in Iran.
Pakistan-mediated peace talks between the US and Iran on April failed to reach a conclusion.

articles.title: Beijing faces its Russia dilemma amid talk of Xi-Trump-Putin summit
articles.summary: China is forced to tread carefully as it considers hosting a meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump. While the optics are sure to favor Moscow, Beijing is risking its image at…

image.caption: Although no government has officially confirmed the meeting, some media outlets have already dubbed it 'the new Yalta'Image: Dmitri Lovetsky/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: An unprecedented meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States could be happening on the sidelines of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen next week.

China has yet to confirm that the meeting will take place. However, a Chinese Foreign Ministry official recently told the press that Beijing was "in communication" with relevant parties. In Moscow, a Kremlin representative said work on "coordination" was underway.

The clearest indication about the potential summit came from US President Donald Trump last weekend. Talking to reporters at a Florida airport, Trump said he "thinks" one of the meetings planned for APEC will be with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Trump, Putin or Xi: Who really runs the world?
Is the world set for a 'new Yalta'?

Despite the lack of official confirmation from either Beijing, Moscow, or Washington, the media has already dubbed the potential trilateral summit a "new Yalta," invoking the optics of the US, UK, and Soviet Union convening at the end of World War II and deciding on the new geopolitical power balance in the Crimean resort town.

blocks.caption: The Yalta summit saw Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill represent the three main victorious powers of WWIIImage: RIA Novosti/SNA/imago

blocks.text: At the same time, nobody seems to be quite sure what the three leaders would talk about if China agrees to host the trilateral summit at APEC.

In his brief remarks to reporters on Sunday, Trump avoided mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine when asked about the possibility of the meeting, bringing up only "Iran" and "denuclearization" as possible talking points.
The Chinese Foreign Ministry reported "no information" when questioned earlier this week about the potential substance of talks.
End of campaign to isolate Putin?

A three-way meeting with a photo op would be a big diplomatic win for Russia's President Putin. Since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Kremlin chief has faced years of diplomatic boycott by Kyiv's allies, most notably the US under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.
Putin first pitched the idea of a trilateral summit last month during a call with Trump. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Putin wanted the meeting to discuss an end to his war in Ukraine.

For the US, the president standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of America's foremost rivals could be a bad look, although Trump has already made a show of personally greeting both leaders with a red carpet at different points during his second term.

As host, China is in an even trickier position. While Russia and China are broadly aligned on many issues, Beijing does not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm China's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.
EU wary of being left out of Ukraine talks

The Chinese government is also working to rebalance economic ties with the EU. The European powers would likely bristle at a summit hosted by China and discussing the war in Ukraine without Kyiv or Brussels present at the table.
Europe seeks role in Ukraine peace talks

"China is clearly uneasy about the possible trilateral meeting with the US and Russia, and although Beijing has shifted its position from saying nothing to admitting that the three powers are in contact, the vagueness of these declarations seems deliberate," Alicja Bachulska, Asia policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW.
"Beijing is aware of the potential negative optics of the 'Yalta 2.0' framing, even if this historical comparison is inaccurate and does not reflect current geopolitical dynamics," Bachulska said.
She notes the trilateral meeting could "trigger further escalation in the already worsening relations between China and the EU" if Ukraine is discussed with no Europeans in the room.

For China, there is also little to gain in terms of optics. Images of Xi standing with Trump, the leader of Beijing's top rival, and Putin, Beijing's partner in opposing the US, could present an awkward look.
"Even if the meeting only yields a photo opportunity, it could nevertheless severely erode China's image," Bachulska added.
Beijing and Moscow stick to 'no limits' partnership
Putin and Xi have met some 40 times since the Chinese president came to power in 2012.

The two neighboring countries have grown especially close following the declaration of "no limits" partnership accord in early 2022. The move was announced by Xi and Putin on the sidelines of Beijing Winter Olympics, just weeks before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The current Russia-China ties are deeper than they have been in decades.
At the core of the axis between the two nations is a long-term strategy to contain US power while fostering an alternative global order both Moscow and Beijing can use for their own ends.
China helping Russia from the sidelines

Throughout the course of the Ukraine war, which is nearing the end of its fifth year with no solution in sight, Beijing has quietly provided Russia with crucial market for energy exports, while supplying technology and so-called "dual-use" goods.
While China did not explicitly provide Russia with weapons, its exports included high-tech components that could be used for modern weapons systems like drones.
Russia needs China trade more than ever
Officially, Beijing maintains neutrality on the Ukraine war and has refused to take responsibility for its outcome.

"China is more interested in reforming global governance in ways that reflect its preferences and red lines while preserving a collegial appearance," Aurelio Insisa, senior analyst at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.
Even if China agrees to host the meeting, it will likely avoid framing it as three top powers making decisions for the rest of the world, according to Insisa.

"Embracing the 'G3' narrative would undermine its image as a champion of the Global South and developing countries. It is also worth noting that Beijing has shown no interest in engaging with the one pressing issue that could realistically be addressed in such a trilateral format: nuclear disarmament," he added.
What are the actual limits of China-Russia axis?
In a report published in August, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC), painted China as a "decisive enabler" of Russia's war in Ukraine.
Beijing was "converting Moscow's dependence into lasting military, technological, economic, and geopolitical advantages while avoiding the obligations of a formal alliance," according to the US body.

However, the commission also noted there were limits to Beijing's strategic support, and intelligence and security concerns remain a constraint on deeper cooperation. The report emphasizes the relationship is more of a strategic alignment than an alliance, with deep mistrust remaining in some key areas.

Russian defense firms, for instance, have accused Chinese companies of stealing intellectual property. Beijing, on the other hand, is concerned with Russia's growing strategic relationship with North Korea, which has reduced Pyongyang's dependence on China.
Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine
China and Russia also differ on nuclear doctrine. While Beijing maintains a longstanding "no first use" policy, Moscow uses nuclear threats as part of its strategy.
China getting a 'privileged vantage point' on Ukraine war
But for now, the benefits of alignment remain.

MERICS' analyst Insisa believes the cooperation between Russia and China will largely continue within this year's framework, including Russia providing energy and potentially transfering military technology in the "few remaining areas where it retains an advantage."

"China, in turn, will continue to supply dual-use technologies, purchase Russian energy, provide Moscow with a measure of diplomatic cover, and — more importantly — offer channels for circumventing Western sanctions," he added.
Notably, China will also get a "privileged vantage point" on how the battlefield in Ukraine is evolving land warfare.
"Strategic distrust between the two sides, particularly Russia's concerns about economic dependence on China, will continue to limit the scope of their cooperation," Insisa said.

articles.title: Cyber attacks and hybrid warfare: Germany gives sweeping powers to its police and intelligence services
articles.summary: Drone sightings and cyberattacks have heightened security concerns. How are the police preparing to meet these challenges? And how do intelligence services plan to counter threats from both domestic…

image.caption: A bomb disposal robot was deployed by police at Germany's Leipzig airport, after a drone was spotted nearbyImage: News5/AFP

blocks.text: Germany's intelligence agencies have been given wide-ranging new powers. The lawmakers in the Bundestag agreed to a reform package on Friday.

Under the new rules, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) will be allowed to respond to cyberattacks by foreign powers with counterattacks of its own. The range of possible measures is broad, from deleting and manipulating data to disabling entire systems and, if necessary, even destroying physical weapons such as drones that could be deployed against Germany.

Under certain conditions, the agencies will also be permitted to enter homes and business premises covertly, for example, to prepare surveillance operations. They will, however, not be allowed to use force against people. An independent oversight board is to be established to monitor the agencies.
Opposition lawmakers specializing in domestic policy warned against granting powers that are too broad.
Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig
Separation of powers hampers procedures

The president of Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), Holger Münch this week again pointed out that today's hybrid attacks pose a new challenge to the organizations safeguarding the country's security. At his organization's annual meeting in Berlin this week, he said the "hybrid attacks" are challenging the "separation principle," which means that the police conduct investigations while intelligence services gather information. The exchange of data between the two is permitted only under strict conditions.

Münch has long objected to this strict division of responsibilities. He has been calling for expanded powers for the police and closer cooperation with the domestic intelligence agency, the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, which is responsible for countering espionage and sabotage.

The separation principle results from lessons learned from the Nazi dictatorship, when the Secret State Police (Gestapo) operated largely outside judicial constraints and served as the regime's central instrument of terror, used to oppress and murder Jews, Sinti and Roma, homosexuals, communists, social democrats, and many others. The Allied powers that defeated Nazi Germany in World War II then decided that the police and intelligence services should remain institutionally separate and be granted different powers.
Germany's spy agency: fact and fiction

Historian Sönke Neitzel of the University of Potsdam considers the separation principle understandable in its historical context. At the BKA's autumn conference, however, he described it as "nonsense" in light of today's threat landscape and said it was no longer necessary in a country that has been a constitutional democracy for decades.

While Neitzel considers the separation principle outdated, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the center-right Christian Social Union (CSU) wants to preserve it in its essential form. In his view, even a more extensive exchange of data does not violate the principle. At the same time, however, he has made clear that he wants to transform the domestically focused Office for the Protection of the Constitution and the foreign intelligence agency, the Federal Intelligence Service(BND), into "real intelligence services."

This legislative reform brings Dobrindt a significant step closer to that goal. Parliament pproved the interior minister's plans with the votes of the governing coalition of the conservative Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the Social Democratic Party (SPD).
As cyberattacks threaten Germany, can Berlin keep data safe?
Espionage, sabotage, and disinformation

Dobrindt insisted that Germany intends to take an active approach to defending itself against cyberattacks: "Anyone who attacks us in this way must know that we are prepared to strike back. They must know that their digital infrastructure, their server infrastructure, and their software will also be targeted by us."

BKA President Holger Münch welcomes Dobrindt's determination and points to the growing threat posed by cyberattacks. The line between criminal and state-sponsored actors is becoming increasingly blurred, he argues. As a result, both intelligence services and law enforcement agencies face the same challenge.

To underscore the scale of the threat as he sees it, Münch cited two statistics: in the first six months of 2026, crime originating from abroad rose by 24% compared with the same period the previous year. What concerns him most is that fewer than 5% of these cases are solved. The BKA chief considers this trend more dangerous than ever: "The state's promise of security can become fragile. Confidence in the ability of its institutions to act effectively and remain steadfast is declining."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Doctor named as DC gym shooting suspect confessed, detailing dispute over living conditions, home manager says
articles.summary:
Gunman killed one person and injured at least four others in and around condo building not far from the White House

More details were emerging on Friday about the previous morning’s

blocks.text: More details were emerging on Friday about the previous morning’s shooting in north-west Washington DC, as a manager at the shooter’s residential building shared how he was angry over living conditions there and confessed to the killings.

The gunman killed one person and injured at least four others on Thursday in and around the condominium building in the Logan Circle neighborhood of the capital, not far from the White House, where he lived.

Police identified the gunman as 55-year-old Matt Lambert, a doctor who had been involved in an ongoing legal dispute with his building’s management. The person killed was identified as James Stuart, 46, a manager at the condominium complex.

According to police, Lambert fatally shot Stuart inside a gym in his building just before 8am ET, before returning to his apartment, where he fired at four people from his balcony. Those victims were taken to hospital, and as of Thursday, one was in critical condition. Lambert then barricaded himself inside his unit, and was found dead with a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Charelle Ferguson, another building manager, recalled speaking with Lambert by phone at around 9am that morning, about an hour after the shooting began, she said in an interview with the Washington Post.

Ferguson told the newspaper that she had been calling residents to check on their safety after shots were fired, when Lambert answered. During the conversation, she said that he told her that he was tired of mold and water damage in his apartment.
“The only way people will pay attention, you have to do something,” Ferguson said he told her. She said that he then confessed over the phone to her to shooting the five people.

“I never thought he’d do something like this,” Ferguson told the Post. She also said that he had previously told her about the issues in his unit, and she said she had been sympathetic to his concerns.

Court records seen by the Guardian show that Lambert sued his condo association in 2025, alleging it had failed to address water damage, mold and moisture issues in his apartment, which he alleged began after exterior work was carried out on the building. The association denied allegations of negligence and denied responsibility for the damage in court filings, and the litigation remained ongoing.
after newsletter promotion

Lambert’s attorney in the civil matter, Joel Braithwaite, said at a news conference on Thursday that he was “deeply shocked” by what happened and that he had last spoken with his client on Tuesday and said that he had sounded fine.
“I can’t tell you how surprised I am because the person I knew as a client is someone who is in the business of healing people,” Braithwaite said.
On Thursday evening, residents gathered at a vigil in the neighborhood, lighting candles and showing support for those affected by the shooting.

blocks.text: The bus was carrying passengers from Bokakhat and was headed towards Nagaon.
Bokakhat is best known as the gateway to Kaziranga National Park, famous for its one-horned rhinoceroses.
Nagaon is an important agricultural and commercial centre in central Assam, about 120km (74.5 miles) west of Bokakhat by road.
Lurinjyoti Gogoi, chief of a regional opposition party, said road safety has long been a major concern in the state.
"The government must take it up seriously," he said.
Road accidents are responsible for thousands of deaths in India every year.
In 2023, 172,000 people lost their lives on Indian roads, or 474 a day – roughly one every three minutes.
The count increased to 183,382 deaths in 2025.
Experts say the crisis is rooted not just in infrastructure but in human behaviour, enforcement gaps and systemic neglect.

articles.title: Ebenezer review: Merry Christmas, Johnny Depp! Is this your comeback yet?
articles.summary: Ebenezer, the latest remake of Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol, isn't terrible. It's also not particularly interesting.

image.caption: Johnny Depp in a scene from Ebenezer. (Jaap Buitendijk/Paramount Pictures)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Ebenezer, the latest remake of Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol, isn't terrible. It's also not particularly interesting.
A Christmas Carol remake fails to justify its existence — even as it avoids complete failure

You're Johnny Depp. Your career — which rests almost entirely on the good will and affection that bubbles to the surface when people hear your name, or at least Captain Jack Sparrow's — is largely in tatters.

A very messy, very public series of allegations of on-set assault (including over a lawsuit you settled) and domestic abuse (which you've denied), along with news-dominating defamation cases, have cumulatively tarnished your golden-goose reputation. Your last big franchise role, as Gellert Grindelwald in Harry Potter's Fantastic Beasts spinoff, ended when Warner Bros. asked you to resign after losing your libel lawsuit with the Sun newspaper for calling you a "wife beater."

You've had few major appearances since. Meanwhile, decades of borderline unbelievable spending sprees saw you acquire a private island and an actual French village (along with nearly enough wine to inebriate the rest of the country) and take on debt rivalling that of some of the world's more spendthrift small nations.
What do you do?

Huh, odd. For your first major Hollywood film since concluding your defamation lawsuit against former partner Amber Heard (a trial you largely won, with Heard ordered to give you $10 million US over her abuse allegations), you've chosen Ebenezer. A beloved if already endlessly rehashed story. To some, this might read as more of a PR campaign than an actually entertaining movie.

On second thought, maybe remaking Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol makes a sort of sense. The tale of our titular, miserly Scrooge learning to love Christmas and his fellow man via visitations from one ghost and three spirits is set in Victorian-era England, after all. You once again get to stumble through London streets covered in grime and soot, speaking in the convincing-to-North Americans, upsetting-to-Brits accent you've cultivated throughout your career.

But as you swagger under meticulously threadbare cloaks and period-specific silly hats, it might be hard for audiences to keep the positive feelings they once felt watching Edward Scissorhands, Sweeney Todd or even Charlie and the Chocolate Factory's Willy Wonka — in your other modern retelling — from resurfacing. They used to like you, didn't they?
This decent-enough return feels a lot like that. Can't they like you again?

items: Apple TV's Nocturne is Nordic noir by the numbers
Wild Horse Nine is a bleak, hopeless sign of the times. You're going to love it

blocks.text: Honestly, this isn't a bad performance. Grimacing and grunting with the best-ish of them, your comedically wide-eyed shrieks and sad-eyed, sentimental monologues pull audiences along Dickens's classic if admittedly saccharine storyline of bitterness to redemption.

This isn't a generational Depp performance, nor is it one with much depth or originality. But it is similar to the stuff you used to do. The idiosyncratic smirk and offhandedly humorous patter that undergirded multibillion-dollar movies is still there. That's worth something, isn't it?

And you still get an all-star cast to back you up: Ian McKellen as your cautionary-tale business partner Jacob Marley, Rupert Grint as your overworked and underpaid underling Bob Cratchit and Tramell Tillman as the foreboding, pagan-like Ghost of Christmas Present.
Tramell Tillman, left, plays the Ghost of Christmas Present to Johnny Depp's Ebenezer Scrooge in Ebenezer. (Jaap Buitendijk/Paramount Pictures)

Each does what they're there for: deliver arch lines from effectively archetypical — and necessarily one-dimensional — characters. They do so with the express purpose of making your unlovable protagonist suffer enough to, by the end, appear sympathetic and humanized and worthy of re-acceptance into society.

In fact, it's all familiar and Johnny Depp-typical enough that you leave audiences half-expecting to see Helena Bonham Carter's face pop up from around every dark, cobblestoned corner. Director Ti West (MaXXXine, Pearl, X) attempts to give the source material his signature campy-horror spin, but instead of the fascinating genre mix of something like Tim Burton's Scissorhands, what we get is closer to an afternoon pantomime.

There are the wanton infusions of rattling chains and moaning spectres straight out of Fleet Street central casting. West's few original interpretations seem to aim for funny while hitting as offensively blunt. For example, instead of Dickens's trembling child-ghosts representing "ignorance" and "want," we get monsters closer to Dr. Seuss's Thing 1 and Thing 2, screeching and chittering along the ground like tiny, see-through ankle-biters from hell.
Redemption roulette

So why did you do it, Johnny? Well if you think about it, relying on this now-cliché story in place of reinvention is perfect for what you need. You're far from the first celebrity actor to inspire "fall from grace" headlines. And in that near-inexhaustible list of attempts to climb back up, there tends to be a unifying element.

There are the less successful attempts. Like Will Smith's painfully self-flagellating Emancipation, about an enslaved man who was so relentlessly and mercilessly beaten that photos of his whip-scarred back helped abolish slavery. Or Kevin Spacey's amateur-looking The Man Who Drew God, about a blind man wrongfully accused of sexually abusing a child. Then there's Armie Hammer's Citizen Vigilante or Jonathan Majors's Run Hide Fight: Infidels — each about a lone man tirelessly battling people the films frame as scum.

There are also more successful comebacks. While Winona Ryder returned from criminal conviction obscurity with a small role in Black Swan, her real re-entry into the spotlight was as the endlessly self-sacrificing and reliable mother in Stranger Things. After earning a reputation for poor performances on set and at the box office, Mickey Rourke made a (temporarily) triumphant return as the beaten and broken but valiant protagonist in The Wrestler.

items: Will Smith's comeback, Emancipation, reduces a slave narrative to an action film
Tom Cruise is fantastic in Digger. You might hate it

blocks.text: Robert Downey Jr. cemented perhaps the most impressive comeback of all time, replacing the public's memory of substance abuse and arrests with his world-saving, devil-may-care billionaire altruist in Iron Man.

Of course, a movie's quality has nothing to do with whether a star is, or isn't, a good person. While not universal, the formula for success is dependable: If you want to rehabilitate a reputation after controversy, frame yourself as the pitiable victim or self-sacrificing hero (or both) in a drama that lightly mirrors your own.

While Ebenezer may be altogether fine — and about as inventive as the novella's entry on "Simple Wikipedia" — it at least serves your needs. Based on a story so effective at commanding good will toward humanity that it essentially established the modern idea of Christmas generosity, what more could you ask for?
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: DOTr: ASEAN Summit-affected airline passengers entitled to refunds, free rebooking
articles.summary: As more travelers head to airports ahead of the long weekend, the Department of Transportation (DOTr) said that passengers whose flights were canceled due to the ASEAN Summit are entitled to a full…

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 10:54pm

As more travelers head to airports ahead of the long weekend, the Department of Transportation (DOTr) said that passengers whose flights were canceled due to the ASEAN Summit are entitled to a full refund, free rebooking, or conversion to a travel fund.
A report by Marisol Abdurahman on “24 Oras” on Friday showed several passengers encountering heavy traffic on their way to the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA).
Among them was Jenny Rose Dasco, who was scheduled to fly to Vietnam on Friday evening.
“Kanina po kasi nahihirapan po ako mag-book ng Grab, and I think almost one hour din po ako nag-book. And after po non kahit sa Skyway po nahirapan po kami makapasok since traffic,” Dasco said.
(Earlier, I had a hard time booking a Grab car, and I think it took me almost an hour to get one. Even after that, we had difficulty getting onto the Skyway because of the traffic.)
Rosie De Guzman, who was traveling to Bacolod with her child, said they anticipated possible traffic congestion due to the ASEAN Summit, prompting them to leave home early.
“Kahit sa Skyway medyo traffic na, madami nang sasakyan… mabuti nga hindi kami na-cancel eh, ‘yung sa [byaheng] Iloilo na-cancel,” De Guzman said.
(Even on the Skyway, traffic was already somewhat heavy, with many vehicles on the road. It was a good thing our flight was not canceled, unlike the flight bound for Iloilo.)
The Civil Aeronautics Board (CAB) issued an advisory listing 264 domestic and 58 international flights across various airlines expected to be affected by the summit from November 13 to 19, 2026.

“These are the things that we are assuring you of, [the] government as well as the airlines— you are assured of either free rebooking, all penalties waived, walang penalty ‘yan, walang rebooking fee, walang kahit ano,” DOTr Secretary Vince Dizon said.

(These are the things that the government and airlines are assuring you of—you are entitled to free rebooking, with all penalties waived. There will be no penalty, rebooking fee, or any other charges.)

“Wala kayong dagdag na babayaran, or full refund, or ‘yung tinatawag na travel fund. Meaning kung gusto mo iwan mo na lang pera mo ibang airline at gamitin mo for future travel, puwede din ‘yun,” he added.
(You will not have to pay anything extra. You can also choose a full refund or what is called a travel fund. This means you can leave your money with the airline and use it for future travel.)
The report also noted an increased presence of security personnel, including police officers, around NAIA.
Despite the influx of travelers, New NAIA Infra Corp. (NNIC) said airport operations remain normal. — Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Indonesia's wiretapping scandal opens a political fault line
articles.summary: Senior police officers are accused of illegally monitoring President Prabowo Subianto, exposing rival networks within Indonesia's security establishment and renewing concerns about political misuse…

image.caption: The surveillance allegedly targeted not just the president, but also ministries, lawmakers, students and others [FILE: September 13, 2026]Image: Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/REUTERS

blocks.text: For decades, Indonesia's police and intelligence agencies have been accused of spying on politicians, journalists, and activists, Now, a widening scandal involving some of the country's most senior police officers has brought those concerns to the heart of government.
Earlier this month, Indonesian police named four senior officers as suspects in an alleged illegal surveillance operation targeting President Prabowo Subianto and other prominent figures.

Former national police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who is not related to the president, was among the senior officers arrested. The ex-police chief became the president's chief of staff in October, just weeks before the scandal broke.
Investigators claim that officers intercepted communications without proper authorization in 2025 and 2026 and then tried to delete records of the operation.

Suyudi Ario Seto, the new police chief, told a parliamentary panel this week that the surveillance targeted the president, officials within the presidential palace, ministries, state institutions, lawmakers, political party figures, governors, anti-corruption officials, activists and students.

A parliamentary commission is investigating the motive behind the wiretapping operation and trying to uncover whether other senior figures were involved. Meanwhile, the police have opened an investigation into possible treason-related offenses.

blocks.caption: Following the wiretapping allegations, President Prabowo hosted ten former chiefs of the national police, along with current Police Chief Suyudi Ario Seto, at his residence for a goodwill meetingImage: Media Team of the President of the Republic of Indonesia

blocks.text: Intensifying political turmoil?
Amnesty International has called for investigations to also determine whether the wiretap operation was used to intimidate government critics and weaken civil liberties.

The government has responded by ordering an additional 20,000 troops to Jakarta as a precaution, although there had been no indication that the wiretap is part of a larger campaign intended to bring down Prabowo's administration.

The affair has intensified tensions between Prabowo and his predecessor, Joko Widodo, commonly known as Jokowi, while exposing deeper problems with the powers and political loyalties of Indonesia's security establishment.
"The use of surveillance is actually pretty widespread," Yohanes Sulaiman, an associate professor at Universitas Jenderal Achmad Yani, told DW.
"While there are laws and regulations, they are flouted since there is no regulation on eavesdropping, especially by law enforcement agencies," he added.

Officially, Indonesia's Electronic Information and Transactions Law prohibits unauthorized interception, while other legislation permits surveillance for specified law enforcement and intelligence purposes.
Despite these safeguards against illegal interception, Sulaiman said it could be argued, "that the police and intelligence are essentially unconstrained."
A long history of surveillance
Indonesia's intelligence agencies and law enforcement have long played a role in political competition, Gatra Priyandita, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, told DW.
Under Suharto's authoritarian New Order regime, which collapsed in 1998, intelligence agencies were central in monitoring political opponents and suppressing dissent.

After democratization, controversies persisted. In 1999, a leaked recording of a telephone conversation involving then-President BJ Habibie raised concerns about surveillance within the presidential palace itself.
In 2024, the elite counterterrorism unit, Densus 88, was caught surveilling Deputy Attorney General Febrie Adriansyah, who at the time was overseeing major corruption investigations.

But what makes the latest allegations particularly significant is "their apparent scale and the suggestion that surveillance capabilities may have been deployed outside established legal procedures and against the sitting president," Priyandita said.

blocks.caption: In 2024, former President Jokowi backed Prabowo's presidential campaign [FILE: November 9, 2023Image: Presidential Secretariat Press Bureau

blocks.text: A delicate moment for the leadership
Since taking office in October 2024, Prabowo, a former special forces general, has sought to consolidate his authority over the country's political and security institutions.
Critics accuse him of accelerating the militarization of civilian government, including through legislation expanding the military's ability to occupy civilian posts.
However, the president inherited a security establishment partly shaped by his predecessor.
In 2024, Jokowi, who couldn't run for office again, backed Prabowo's presidential campaign and his eldest son, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, became Prabowo's running mate and subsequently vice president.
The Jokowi-Prabowo alliance was decisive for Prabowo's electoral victory, but it also left him governing alongside officials and political networks cultivated during Jokowi's decade in power.
On Thursday, Jokowi's son Gibran resigned as vice president amid a growing controversy over his educational credentials.

Indonesia's Constitutional Court and the country's Supreme Court found that Gibran's overseas high school qualifications fell short of legal requirements for vice presidential candidates, and had been wrongly accepted by election authorities.
The academic credentials probe was apparently not related to the investigations into the wiretapping scandal.
Can Indonesia reform its security establishment?

A series of government reshuffles in recent months has also been interpreted as Prabowo's attempt to strengthen his control, especially against some Jokowi loyalists. Listyo, appointed police chief by Jokowi in 2021 and long regarded as close to the former president, was replaced in October.

"Prabowo may have consolidated his political authority since taking office, but that does not necessarily translate into complete control over institutions whose senior leadership and internal networks were shaped under the previous Jokowi government," Priyandita said.

Also, Prabowo may emerge politically stronger if the investigation weakens rival networks within the police. However, replacing one set of political loyalties with another would do little to resolve the underlying problem in the country's security apparatus.

blocks.caption: Gibran Rakabuming Raka stepped down from his role as vice president this week [FILE: May 20, 2026]Image: Willy Kurniawan/REUTERS

blocks.text: The controversy has renewed calls for reforms that would prevent police surveillance capabilities from becoming instruments of political competition.
'Systematic abuse of power'

Because the latest wiretapping controversy targeted not only the president but also political elites and key civil society actors, "surveillance goes beyond mere politics," Nicky Fahrizal, a researcher at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Jakarta, told DW.
"It is a calculated and systematic abuse of power," he added.
Fahrizal argued that a fundamental problem lies in the National Police's constitutional and institutional position, which answers directly to the president.
This increases the risk that the police respond to presidential political interests rather than solely to the law.
In November last year, Prabowo established a police reform commission to investigate longstanding concerns about professionalism, governance, and accountability.
However, Fahrizal said former police chief Listyo failed to implement meaningful reforms, with the latest allegations showing the consequences of inadequate oversight.

Fahrizal called for Indonesia to bring its fragmented surveillance regulations together under a unified legal framework, with tighter controls over the interception powers of the police's Criminal Investigation Agency and the Intelligence and Security Agency.
"Internal police reform must urgently address this by restoring professionalism and a proper institutional ethos," Fahrizal said.
Without such changes, divided political loyalties risk becoming a "dangerous virus" spreading through the police and other security institutions, he added.

articles.title: Banned books from Ireland’s room of ‘evil literature’ finally see the light of day
articles.summary:
Censored books spanning 1926-96 contained themes ‘likely to corrupt or deprave’, or references to contraception or violence

For almost a century, an Irish government building in the heart of…

blocks.text: For almost a century, an Irish government building in the heart of Dublin has hosted a secret sanctum: the banned books room.
The department of justice, on St Stephen’s Green, did not grant public access, because the shelves contained 12,000 books deemed indecent or obscene.
It was a graveyard for titles condemned by the Censorship of Publications Board, a guardian of public morals which guillotined anything that smelled of sex or other corruptions.
Harold Robbins was interred. So too Ian Fleming, Edna O’Brien, Brendan Behan, Oscar Wilde, DH Lawrence, JD Salinger, John Updike, Iris Murdoch, F Scott Fitzgerald and many more.

blocks.caption: Books previously banned in Ireland that were held at the department of justice are to be moved to the National Archives. Photograph: Ireland’s department of justice, home affairs and migration

blocks.text: Exhumation, however, is nigh. The entire collection is to be moved to the National Archives as part of the repeal of Ireland’s censorship laws. The censors’ notes, minutes and ledgers that detail why each book was banned will be made publicly available for the first time – a trove for researchers of social history and state control.

“The censors prohibited works that they saw as contravening or subverting public morality – anything that was seen as unwholesome or suggestive of sexual immorality,” said Orlaith McBride, the director of the National Archives. “It was often just the innuendo of something that could have been perceived as likely to corrupt or deprave.”

blocks.caption: Notes and ledgers from Ireland’s Censorship of Publications Board are to be made available to the public at the National Archives. Photograph: Ireland’s department of justice, home affairs and migration

blocks.text: The volumes span 1926 to 1996 and encompass pulp fiction, high-brow literature and academic texts. References to family planning, contraception and violence were likely to elicit bans, said McBride.

So too did suggestive imagery, such as the cover of O’Brien’s groundbreaking 1960 novel, The Country Girls. “It’s very subtly done but you can see the contours of the female form. The issue wasn’t just the contents but the image,” McBride said.

Banned titles included classics such as Wilde’s The Picture of Dorian Gray, Behan’s Borstal Boy and Lawrence’s Lady Chatterley’s Lover, as well as pulpy paperbacks with titles such as The Baby Doll Murders, A Doctor and his Mistress and Torrid Tale of a Wicked Town.

Scholarly tomes such as Sexual Life in England Past and Present and arcane works such as The Collected Works of Pierre Louÿs, a Belgian poet of the early 20th century, also ended up in what was informally called the banned books room.

blocks.caption: Torrid titles? The banned books encompass pulp fiction, high-brow literature and academic texts. Photograph: Ireland’s department of justice, home affairs and migration

blocks.text: The censorship board adopted a broad definition of indecent and obscene, said Brian Hughes, a history lecturer at the University of Limerick’s Mary Immaculate College.
after newsletter promotion

“I think people would be very surprised seeing these books or reading some of these books to think that they were banned at all in the first place, because attitudes are quite different now. I think it suggests that certainly in terms of printed matter, the written word, there’s a much more liberal society. It is a more secular society as well; that’s part of it. But I think it’s a wider process of attitudes towards sex, sexuality changing.”

In 1926, soon after independence, the nascent Irish Free State established the Committee of Evil Literature, a five-man panel tasked with protecting public morals. It recommended a strict system of vetting that led to the Censorship of Publications Board – which, for a time, was led by a Catholic priest – and an appeals board.
The censors reviewed material that was submitted by members of the public and customs and revenue officers. They also sourced books through a subscription to the Times Book Club.

blocks.caption: Minutes of a meeting in 1959 of Ireland’s Censorship of Publications Board. Photograph: Ireland’s department of justice, home affairs and migration.

blocks.text: The periodicals and books that accumulated at what is now known as the department of justice, home affairs and migration will be moved after Christmas to the National Archives, where they will be conserved, catalogued and stored.

“Many are first editions, and because of sheer age in a vulnerable state, so they won’t be available to the public,” said McBride. People could source them online “and in all good bookshops”, she said.

The censors’ registers and notes, plus letters from the public and interest groups, were transferred this week, and are undergoing conservation in advance of becoming publicly available. McBride said: “They are the most interesting because they record the decisions and reveal the thinking behind the bans.”

articles.title: Sara Duterte defense seen to end presentation within November: What next?
articles.summary: The pace at which the defense panel of Vice President Sara Duterte is presenting its witnesses in her impeachment trial makes it likely that it will finish presenting its case before the end of…

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 10:03pm

The pace at which the defense panel of Vice President Sara Duterte is presenting its witnesses in her impeachment trial makes it likely that it will finish presenting its case before the end of November, the spokesman of the tribunal has said.

According to Sandra Aguinaldo's report on "24 Oras," the defense panel will have ten days to file its formal offer of evidence after it wraps up its presentation of witnesses. The prosecution will also have ten days to comment or file its opposition to the defense's case.

"Kung makikita natin sa bilis ng pagpepresenta ng mga witnesses po, ay nakaabot po tayo ng 3-4 witnesses in a day for the presentation for the defense. Ganun din po ‘yung ine-expect natin na time and motion na mangyayari sa mga succeeding hearing days,” Tongol said.

(Looking at the pace of the witness presentations, we have reached three to four witnesses a day for the defense's presentation. That is the same timeline and pace we expect to see in the succeeding hearing days.)
The court will then resolve on the formal offer and the comments within 10 days at most, according to the impeachment court spokesperson.
Verdict seen before Christmas
Atty. Paolo Panelo, Duterte’s spokesperson, explained why the Vice President’s camp expects the verdict to be handed down before the Christmas break.

“Ang sabi niya sa akin noon, ang parang pakay ng mga nagmamadali para habulin itong Christmas break ay para daw kung may conviction at magalit ‘yung mga tao, hindi sila makapag-express masyado ng galit nila dahil Pasko na at kung acquittal naman, eh di makakalimutan na sa susunod na taon, so ‘yun ang impormasyon na natanggap niya,” Panelo said.

(What she told me before was that the apparent motive of those rushing to beat the Christmas break is so that if there is a conviction and people get angry, they won't be able to express their outrage as much because it's already Christmas—and if it's an acquittal, it will simply be forgotten by next year. So that is the information she received.)
For its part, the prosecution said it also appears feasible to wrap up the impeachment proceedings before Christmas.

“We've been dwelling on this for three years already, and I think it's about time we put an end to this by witnessing the verdict as to whether it is conviction or acquittal at least before Christmas,” lead prosecutor Congressman Gerville Luistro said.
The next proceedings for Duterte’s impeachment trial are scheduled for November 19 to 20, after which the Senate will take a break from the trial to focus on the 2027 national budget.
The next trial day is expected to resume on December 1. –Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/NB, GMA News
