articles.title: DepEd issues stronger work immersion guidelines for SHS students
articles.summary: The Department of Education (DepEd) on Friday said that it was strengthening its work immersion program for senior high school students by issuing renewed guidelines.

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 9:53pm
The Department of Education (DepEd) on Friday said that it was strengthening its work immersion program for senior high school students by issuing renewed guidelines.
This comes as the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) recorded a lower youth employment rate in September 2026. Many young workers have also reported that it was harder to look for more work.

“Ang work immersion ang makakapaghanda sa ating mga mag-aaral para mas maging job-ready sila, kaya mas malaki ang chance na agad makahanap ng trabaho ang graduates ng Grade 12,” DepEd Secretary Sonny Angara said in a statement.
(Work immersion prepares our students to be job-ready so there is a bigger chance for Grade 12 graduates to look for work.)

“May mga kausap na tayong partners sa industriya para sa mga guaranteed placement sa kanilang work immersion. Based on experience, the chances of employment are higher when they undergo a longer immersion period with the company or organization,” he added.

(We are speaking with partners in the industry so that there is guaranteed placement in their work immersion. Based on experience, the chances of employment are higher when they undergo a longer immersion period with the company or organization.)

DepEd Order No. 023, s. 2026 forms part of the Strengthened Senior High School (SSHS) Curriculum, and it aims to make practical learning more relevant to a learner’s chosen industry. Under the guidelines, work immersion is mandatory in the Technical-Professional (TechPro) Track.
TechPro students are required to undergo either a 320-hour one-term model or a 540- to 640-hour two-term model, depending on the school’s capacity.
Work immersion for learners in the Academic Track is still optional. Those who are interested, however, are allowed to undertake a 320-hour program after they complete their prerequisite electives.
Academic Track students may also take an 80-hour Field Exposure elective to explore possible career paths.
Arts Apprenticeship also allows students interested in creative fields to explore visual arts, media arts, performing arts, and more.
According to the DepEd, schools must assess and screen partner institutions and formalize agreements. Students must not be assigned tasks for free labor.
The work immersion activities must not surpass eight hours a day per day and five days a week, with the school being required to have regular check-in sessions with the students.
Aside from private companies, schools are also urged to partner with government units and agencies.

DepEd said that the guidelines will apply to public and private SSHS pilot implementers starting in the school year 2026-2027. The remaining senior high schools will implement the guidelines starting in 2027. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: ASEAN Summit to tackle transnational crime, food security measures
articles.summary: As the Philippines wraps up its chairmanship of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit, several key measures are expected to be finalized to address challenges facing member…

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 9:45pm

As the Philippines wraps up its chairmanship of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit, several key measures are expected to be finalized to address challenges facing member states.
The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Friday said these measures aim to address issues including the impacts of the Middle East crisis, food security, and transnational crimes.

"Given the situation at the moment, we are still feeling the impacts of the Middle East crisis, so we should expect some additional measures and decisions from our leaders in addressing the energy situation that we're facing at the moment," Foreign Affairs Assistant Secretary Dominic Xavier "Dax" Imperial, spokesperson for ASEAN Affairs, said in a press briefing.
"We will also expect some decisions and measures with regard to more protection and welfare of migrant workers, especially the Filipino migrant workers," he added.

On November 14, DFA Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro will convene the ASEAN foreign ministers for their final meeting, where they will review and decide on the implementation of the ASEAN Five-Point Consensus, as one of the agenda items.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will chair the ASEAN Summit and related summits from November 15 to 17.

The program on November 15 will start with an opening ceremony followed by the plenary and retreat sessions. It will culminate with the interface meetings with the ASEAN Interparliamentary Assembly, the ASEAN Business Advisory Council, and ASEAN youth.
The Plus One summits will be held from November 16-17.
On November 17, Marcos will convene the 29th ASEAN Plus Three Summit and the 21st East Asia Summit. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Industry disruption continues: GMA’s profit falls 98% in Q3, ABS-CBN still in red
articles.summary: GMA cites the 'continued shift of audiences and advertising budgets from traditional media to digital platforms' and the 'challenging business environment' for its disappointing earnings

blocks.text: GMA cites the 'continued shift of audiences and advertising budgets from traditional media to digital platforms' and the 'challenging business environment' for its disappointing earnings

items: GMA Network reported a 98% decline in net income for Q3 2026, dropping from P2 billion to P32.85 million, attributed to decreased advertising revenue and a challenging business environment.
Despite the financial downturn, GMA remains the leading television station in the Philippines, with strong ratings for its top programs and continued growth in digital advertising revenues.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines’ broadcast industry leader GMA Network (GMA) disclosed a steep 98% fall in net income in the third quarter of 2026, while its erstwhile competitor ABS-CBN reported it was still deep in the red.

In its earnings disclosure on Friday, November 13, publicly listed GMA saw its net income spiral down from P2 billion in Q3 2025 to only P32.85 million in Q3 2026. Revenues fell 31%, or by P4.3 billion, in the same period. EBITDA was also “significantly lower,” dropping 68% from P4.5 billion to P1.4 billion.

blocks.caption: Screenshot from GMA Network’s disclosure on November 13, 2026.

blocks.text: “The downturn was attributable to the absence of political advocacies and advertisements in relation to the 2025 mid-term election as well as softening of recurring revenues year-on-year,” the company said.

Advertising revenue was the main culprit, declining 33% or from P12.8 billion in Q3 2025 to P8.6 billion in Q3 2026, but GMA also cited the “continued shift of audiences and advertising budgets from traditional media to digital platforms” for the disappointing performance.

Aside from industry disruption, it also noted the “challenging business environment marked by elevated fuel prices, persistent inflation, supply chain disruptions, rising labor and utility costs, and ongoing geopolitical uncertainties stemming from the Middle East conflict.”
“These conditions drove up production and distribution costs, squeezed profit margins, and prompted businesses to exercise greater caution in their advertising expenditures,” the network said.

GMA’s poor earnings wouldn’t be a big surprise if it hadn’t kept its industry leadership. But, in fact, GMA was still the top television station in the whole country in the first three quarters, based on Nielsen TV Audience Measurement data.
Among its top TV programs were Kapuso Mo, Jessica Soho, and its flagship 24 Oras nightly news show. Its radio stations, Super Radyo DZBB and Barangay LS 97.1, are also ahead in ratings.

GMA’s digital business continues to be a key contributor to revenues, with digital advertising revenues providing the company’s “second largest revenue contributor,” signaling the continued rise of digital platforms.

Meanwhile, still Lopez-led ABS-CBN Corporation, which lost its lucrative broadcast business in 2020 no thanks to the Duterte administration, reported a consolidated net loss of P2.95 billion in Q3 2026 compared to P2.24 billion in Q3 2026, a decline of 32%. (READ: The secret to the Lopez family’s enduring control of ABS-CBN)

blocks.caption: Screenshot from ABS-CBN’s disclosure on November 13, 2026.

blocks.text: Total revenues fell by 11% from P11.75 billion in Q3 2025, an election year, to P10.5 billion in Q3 2026.

“The Company continued to face a challenging market environment into the 3rd quarter. Global economic and geopolitical developments, the pace of domestic economic growth and subdued consumer and business sentiment weighed on advertising and subscription demand in both segments,” the pre-2020 broadcast industry leader said.

ABS-CBN, which produces and sells entertainment content to foreign audiences, said growth in licensing and international syndication (plus co-production revenues) “offset the decrease in advertising and other consumer revenue streams.”

blocks.caption: Industry disruption continues: GMA’s profit falls 98% in Q3, ABS-CBN still in red

blocks.text: A movie starring ABS-CBN’s popular DonBelle love team, Donnie Pangilinan and Belle Mariano, and the Philippines’ top girl group, BINI, were big contributors to the company’s revenues during the period.

“Star Cinema released Tayo Sa Wakas in May 2026, and BINI’s world tour began in June 2026 after the group’s April appearance at the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival. ABS-CBN Global staged 27 events across international markets, including ASAP XP Australia, which featured two sold-out performances in July. These further contributed to the Group’s revenue growth,” ABS-CBN said.

blocks.caption: Industry disruption continues: GMA’s profit falls 98% in Q3, ABS-CBN still in red

blocks.text: ABS-CBN strongly pivoted to digital after it lost its franchise more than six years ago. It also now sells content to its former competitors, GMA and TV5, or partners with them to produce shows.
ABS-CBN recently got a capital infusion from new investors, which is helping the company survive the industry disruption. – Rappler.com

articles.title: New York is running out of room for its waste even with Statue of Liberty sized landfill
articles.summary:
One company is proposing elongating the life of the dump, pungent smell and all, several more decades

As a visual representation of how

blocks.text: As a visual representation of how New York is running out of places to put its waste, the largest active landfill in the state is a striking one. The hulking Seneca Meadows landfill is already the height of the Statue of Liberty and its operators are seeking to raise it even further, to the consternation of nearby residents.

The landfill, situated in the scenic Finger Lakes region in the northern reaches of New York state, has grown since the 1980s to now sprawl across 350 acres of deposited trash, mounded up to the height of around 300ft – roughly the same height of the Statue of Liberty.

“All around the lakes is pretty flat until you see this monster of a hill,” said Mark Pitifer, a marketing administrator at Waterloo Containers, a glass packaging company that sits next to the landfill and is dwarfed by its neighbor. “I mean it’s incredible, it’s like being in downtown New York City only instead of a building, it’s trash.”

Locals in the nearby towns of Waterloo and Seneca Falls, the latter famed as the birthplace of the women’s rights movement in the US, had hoped the bulging landfill would be closed when its permit expired last year. But the operator, Texas-based Waste Connections, has proposed elongating the life of the landfill for several more decades via 47 acres of newly lined disposal cells and adding another 70ft to the trash heap’s height.

As New York state authorities mull whether to grant this expansion, the landfill has become a central point of grievance over the pungent smell, water pollution and planet-heating pollution given off by the places we dump our rubbish. Seneca Meadows is now the largest source of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, in the state, according to a study last year based on researchers using aircraft measurements.
The operator, Waste Connections, did not respond to questions from the Guardian; it defends its environmental protections measures and record in statements on its website.

The increasing size of landfills also raises uncomfortable questions about how much waste we produce and what to do with it. Seneca Meadows receives around 6,000 tons of trash each day from across New York, with 1,500 of those tons originating from New York City, which sends its rubbish to landfills hundreds of miles away that are rapidly filling up and are set to be completely full within the next 16 to 25 years.

If burning rubbish or casually dumping it into rivers and the ocean is too environmentally harmful, what is to be done with our waste beyond continually supersizing landfills to the point they become a major climate, as well as local, hazard?

“We are at the precipice of a crisis,” said Emily Gallagher, a Democratic member of the New York state assembly who recently took a tour of the Seneca Meadows site and has convened a hearing on the state’s waste storage policies.

“There is this huge mountain of trash that is off gassing almost 24 hours a day … contaminating the Finger Lakes, contaminating the groundwater,” she said of the site. “People we met in town are in really bad shape, we need to shut this expansion attempt down now.”

Gallagher said intense lobbying and donations from interests aligned with the plastics and fossil fuels industries has stymied strict measures to reduce waste and enforce more recycling – she estimated 80% of the Seneca Meadows contents could be recycled. But she added there needed to be a broader societal reckoning with the tsunami of trash, much of it from cheap and disposal items, we create.

“We say throwing away but there is no away,” said Gallagher, whose district includes a part of New York City’s borough of Brooklyn. “The problem is that it will take a culture change that people won’t want to do until it is forced in their faces. We used to have a much more circular economy, where people reused and rewashed everything, but we have been indoctrinated into a convenience culture, even if it then causes us more inconvenience.”

Dealing with trash is “gross problem”, Gallagher acknowledged. “But we need a much deeper conversation about it rather than continuously pushing it to the side because it’s uncomfortable and it confronts our human desire for comfort and our laziness,” she added.

The municipal government of New York City has pointed to recent efforts to reduce its waste, such as the pickup and composting of organic matter, which makes up around a third of what is left as trash in the city.

Yet New York City residents still create around 12,000 tons of trash a day and it will need to go somewhere. The city does not send residential trash to Seneca Meadows – although some private contractors do – but will be sending it further and further from the city, which has not hosted its own waste for several decades.

“As capacity continues to shrink in the region, we will likely export trash to further locations,” said a spokesman for the city’s sanitation department. “Our commitment to rail export makes this much easier than trucking.”
Yvonne Taylor, co-founder of Seneca Lake Guardian environmental group, stressed she didn’t want other communities to suffer living near growing landfills like hers had.

Residents routinely text her to say that they have had to remove their children from the nearby school because the smell had sickened them, or of ruined outdoor birthday parties and other gatherings, she said. Pitifer, of Waterloo Containers, said the company has had to install filtration equipment to help employees deal with the overpowering stench of the landfill.

“We don’t need to use plastic grocery bags, we don’t need to use plastic toothbrushes, toothpaste, shampoo bottles, and laundry detergent bottles – all of those things can be packaged in other materials that don’t wind up in a landfill,” said Taylor.
“So the solutions are out there. We just need the political capital to turn this around.” In the meantime, though, the Seneca Meadows expansion must be halted, she said.

“We certainly don’t want to push this burden onto another community and say, “Oh, we just don’t want it here. You guys take it.” That’s not our philosophy at all,” Taylor said. “Our philosophy is that we need to start somewhere, and that somewhere is with Seneca Meadows.”
The New York state department of environmental conservation and Waste Connections were both contacted for comment and did not respond.
Waste Connections says on its website that it is “dedicated to the preservation and advancement of the environment” and has an “exemplary compliance record”.

Its environmental protections include a “double composite liner” and a collection system for rainwater that has contacted waste. Landfill gas is captured and burned to generate electricity, it says, and there is ‘state of the art’ equipment and practices to capture odors which it says air monitoring data shows is effective. It says the gas is 50 per cent methane and it is collected and controlled, and the system is monitored to evaluate its effectiveness.

articles.title: UN watchdog 'increasingly concerned' over Iran nuclear site
articles.summary: It says it has never been able to inspect a uranium enrichment plant at Isfahan which Iran announced over a year ago.

blocks.text: The UN's nuclear watchdog has said it is "increasingly concerned" about a nuclear facility in Iran which it has not been allowed to inspect.

Iran informed the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) of plans to set up the uranium enrichment plant in the city of Isfahan a day before Israel began attacking its nuclear sites last June. The US joined the strikes later that month.
In a report seen by news agencies, the IAEA said it does not know the exact location or whether it contains nuclear material.
Since the start of the latest war, Iran has restricted IAEA inspectors' access to its nuclear sites, preventing the agency from verifying its enriched uranium stockpile.
Under a 2015 nuclear deal, Iran agreed to limit its enriched uranium stockpile to 300kg and enrichment to 3.67% purity. It subsequently exceeded both.
Before the June 2025 strikes, it had accumulated an estimated 441kg enriched to 60%, close to weapons grade.
The nuclear complex at Isfahan suffered extensive damage in US and Israeli strikes, particularly the parts above the ground. The condition of its underground facilities is not clear.
The IAEA believes much of Iran's highly enriched uranium was stored there.

"The Agency's lack of information about [Iran's] nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern... and needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency," it said in the latest report.
Iran announced plans for the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP) on 12 June 2025, shortly after an IAEA resolution which declared Iran had failed to meet its nuclear safeguards obligations.
Iran initially agreed to allow inspectors to visit the facility, but the inspection was cancelled after Israel launched attacks the following day.

The IAEA's latest calls come almost a year after it made a similar appeal to Iran. At the time it said it had only inspected some of the 13 nuclear facilities that were "unaffected" by the attacks and none of the seven that were.

The US and Israel said they attacked Iran's nuclear sites to prevent it developing nuclear weapons - something Iran has consistently denied seeking. It says its nuclear programme is for peaceful civilian purposes only.

articles.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
articles.summary: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms has cast doubt on Anthropic's looming IPO. Yet, with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.

image.caption: Anthropic is aiming for a valuation of more than $1 trillion when it goes public next weekImage: Carlos Barria/REUTERS

blocks.text: 2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar artificial intelligence (AI) bet started paying off. Instead, it’s turning into a test of nerves.
In the first half of the year, many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.
Two of the largest AI players — Anthropic and OpenAI — announced plans for public listings, following SpaceX's much-hyped IPO in June, which briefly made Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire.
AI models, meanwhile, got noticeably better at difficult tasks in the race to beat human intelligence.
Post-midterm AI sell-off rattles global markets amid Big Tech jitters
AI doubts trigger market turbulence

The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty. While the stock of Nvidia, a chipmaker, pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen their stock prices gyrate wildly.

Then last week, after the Democrats secured control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections, technology stocks sold off dramatically, with the Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — losing more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.

In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit this week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days. The sell-off followed news that Nvidia's board — alongside the FBI — is investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s ties to a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.
On Thursday, Huang resigned from the chipmaker when a second alleged marital affair was revealed, sending Nvidia's shares lower still.

blocks.caption: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is under scrutiny over an affair with an alleged Chinese spyImage: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Amid huge spending, big returns remain elusive

Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending. Growing pressure on US lawmakers to curb the expansion of AI data centers has added to those doubts.
In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.

"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, told DW, meaning that times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "show me the money."
Fears that Democrats could regulate AI lead to global market bloodbath
AI stocks needed a 'healthy correction'

Other analysts think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks last week's rout was a "healthy correction."
"We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie."

In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.
Questions over timing of Anthropic IPO

While OpenAI has delayed its public listing until next year, Claude-maker Anthropic still plans its IPO later this month. On Tuesday, the company said it would offer 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 per share.
Dick said Anthropic’s decision to go ahead amid the market sell-off left him scratching his head. “Is this the best timing?” he asked.
While Anthropic had originally targeted a valuation of over $2 trillion, it now thinks the firm could be worth around $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion.
Dick said the valuation depends on whether Anthropic can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of over $600 billion in revenue by 2030.

"If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued."
Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude-maker's prospects.

“Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company,” Seth told Bloomberg this week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. “Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize.”
Signs to watch, not reasons to flee

With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

There are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported last week.
"They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs."
That has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to issue new AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have announced deals worth $67 billion.
Rees said another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers.

This summer, New York and Texas temporarily paused new data center approvals. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat who takes office in January, wants new laws to stop data centers’ heavy power and water use from pushing up household bills.
Why US voters are fighting Trump's AI data center boom
Not 'different this time'

In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railroads, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.

When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.
Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.
"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.

articles.title: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
articles.summary: Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself.

blocks.text: How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?
The answer is very.

The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.

Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.

Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.

But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.

Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.
But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.

The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president.

US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?
That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections.
A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny.
Other senior officials wanted a tougher response. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist.

There were also questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department.

This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle.
Now the political pressure is building.

Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach.
And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure.

Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.
Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors.
The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.
It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history".
That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out.

There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long?
The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump.

The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns.
This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department.

Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself. How much influence did he have? What did the president know? And who was ultimately responsible for protecting America's most sensitive technology?

articles.title: Sandiganbayan declares Zaldy Co’s 3 co-accused as fugitives
articles.summary: The three are facing graft and malversation charges over alleged irregularities in the procurement and construction of a P289.4-million flood control project in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro

blocks.text: ANTI-GRAFT COURT. The Sandiganbayan in Quezon City.
Jansen Romero/Rappler
The three are facing graft and malversation charges over alleged irregularities in the procurement and construction of a P289.4-million flood control project in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro
MANILA, Philippines – The Sandiganbayan Fifth Division has declared three co-accused of dismissed Ako Bicol representative Zaldy Co as fugitives.

In its ruling on Tuesday, November 10, the anti-graft court named Sunwest board members Anthony Ngo and Consuelo Aldon, and Department of Public Works and Highways Mimaropa materials engineer Timogen Sacar as fugitives. The court said they had demonstrated “an unmistakable intent to evade warrants and avoid prosecution.”

The three are facing graft and malversation charges over alleged irregularities in the procurement and construction of a P289.4-million flood control project in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro. The allegedly defective project was first exposed by Oriental Mindoro Governor Humerlito “Bonz” Dolor.

blocks.caption: Flood control anomalies: The case of Oriental Mindoro

blocks.text: According to prosecutors, the three remain at large despite the issuance of arrest warrants on November 21, 2025, nearly a year ago.

“Given the high-profile nature of the case, it is reasonable to conclude that the accused are aware of the criminal proceedings and the outstanding warrants issued against them. Thus, by staying beyond the reach of law enforcement while fully aware of pending warrants of arrest confirms accused’s deliberate intent to evade the judicial process,” the Sandiganbayan said.
Co, the beneficial owner of Sunwest, also remains at large despite facing multiple cases. He reportedly fled the country.
Sunwest was identified by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. as one of the top flood control contractors under his administration.
The Sandiganbayan also ordered the cancellation of the passports of Ngo, Aldon, and Sacar to prevent them from seeking refuge overseas.

“Removing the official travel document necessary for the fugitive to leave the country or to travel between foreign countries hinders the attempts to evade judicial process,” the court said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Iran says it destroyed US military radar in Bahrain in retaliatory strike
articles.summary:
First direct attack on US military installations for months was in response to US airstrike on communications tower

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and…

blocks.text: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain – its first direct attack on US military installations for months – in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz.

“This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.”

Donald Trump has said in a series of media interviews over the past 24 hours that he will attack Iran only if necessary, claiming that Gulf countries such as Saudi Arabia have urged him to hold back from planned large-scale military strikes.
Trump announced that he had asked his vice-president, JD Vance, to end his interest in negotiating a new deal with Iran and instead focus on corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.

Vance had been seen by the Iranians as the most trustworthy figure close to Trump, but they had rejected his request for a personal meeting with their negotiators to discuss the terms of a peace deal.

Vance has been in the forefront of Republicans saying the war led to the massive Republican losses in the midterms. Trump said he had been disappointed in the American public, since higher diesel prices was a small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

An opinion poll in the UK shows 65% of the British public would oppose the US resuming the war in Iran, and only 14% would back it. The poll was conducted by YouGov for the Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu).
It also found 54% oppose UK bases being used by the US to mount attacks on Iran, with 29% in favour. Support for additional UK sanctions against Iran was found to be 45%, with 22% opposed.

The poll was conducted on Tuesday and Wednesday this week, before two Iranians were found guilty on Thursday of spying and planning attacks on journalists in the UK. The Iranian embassy has rejected the court judgment as an attempt to advance a political agenda.

Chris Doyle, the director of Caabu, said: “The British public are sceptical about any war on Iran and what it might achieve. What might make the Burnham government take note is the very high level of opposition to any further war amongst 2024 Labour voters, at 79%.”

Iran’s Assembly of Experts, a body of elected Islamic jurists responsible for choosing the supreme leader, has become the first governing institution in Iran to call for a review of the country’s defence doctrine, potentially leading to religious permission for Iran to try to acquire a nuclear weapon.

In a statement released on Thursday, the assembly called for reviewing Iran’s membership of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, describing the move as an “unavoidable necessity” and a “public and national demand”.

The intervention carries a religious as much as political significance because the 88-strong assembly comprises senior clerics, most of whom are supposed to be qualified to exercise independent Islamic legal reasoning.

Iran has had a longstanding prohibition on nuclear weapons, based on a fatwa issued by the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, but the relevance of the fatwa in the wake of the US attacks on Iran has been questioned widely inside political and security circles.
Whether Iran has the stockpiles of uranium or technology to build a nuclear weapon is contested.

The UN nuclear inspectorate has expressed alarm about a continued lack of information from Iran about its nuclear sites. It said: “Our concerns are growing over Iran’s refusal to allow access to design information or inspections of the Isfahan facility. We do not know the exact location of the Isfahan uranium enrichment facility or whether it contains nuclear materials. It is imperative that we carry out our verification activities in Iran without further delay.”

articles.title: Parents of autistic teen detained by Alberta RCMP demand release of delayed watchdog report
articles.summary: The parents of an autistic teenager who was arrested at an Alberta playground and detained by RCMP four years ago are calling for the results of a watchdog investigation to be released.

image.caption: Ryley Bauman and his mother, Laura Hawthorne, are seen here at an Edmonton playground shortly after he was handcuffed by RCMP in St. Albert in 2022. His family is hoping a watchdog investigation will offer answers and accountability. (David Bajer/CBC)

blocks.text: The parents of an autistic teenager who was arrested at an Alberta playground and detained by RCMP four years ago are calling for the results of a watchdog investigation to be released.
Ryley Bauman was 16 in October 2022 when he was seized from a St. Albert playground and placed in holding cells by RCMP, who believed he was an adult intoxicated by drugs or alcohol.

A previous Alberta watchdog investigation found that Bauman — who is non-verbal and functions at the level of a seven-year-old — repeatedly harmed himself in custody, was held down by officers, sedated and taken to hospital before RCMP learned he had been reported missing by family.

Weeks later, the RCMP Civilian Review and Complaints Commission (CRCC) launched an investigation into his detention to determine if new policies are needed to improve interactions between RCMP and neurodivergent people.

The CRCC promised to examine if officers properly accommodated Bauman’s disability and took reasonable steps to prevent him from harming himself, and if adequate training is provided to help police distinguish intoxication from disabilities.

Four years later, Bauman’s parents Laura Hawthorne and Aaron Krause are still waiting to learn if the CRCC will recommend disciplining the arresting officers or changing RCMP policies in their son’s name.
'Falling through the cracks'
“They can hide behind paperwork and blow off deadlines and it's been over four years and we've just watched Ryley deteriorate,” said Hawthorne in an interview with CBC News.
“I'm never going to let go of this. We're never going to go away because this is just the last straw. When it comes to falling through the cracks, Ryley deserves more.”
Krause said Canada's RCMP watchdog system is fraught with delays, calling bodies like the CRCC flawed and “jawless” when it comes to holding officers accountable.

“Ryley deserves not just justice for what happened to him, but Ryley deserves changes inside of the RCMP's operating system, inside of their own protocols, and how they address and react to people that have neurodivergence,” Krause said.
“There shouldn't be a massive bureaucratic red-tape nightmare preventing an organization that is supposed to protect people from admitting that it made a mistake.”

items: National RCMP watchdog launches review into arrest of Alberta teen with autism
Parents of autistic teen arrested by Alberta RCMP call for charges, improved training

blocks.text: In a statement Monday, CRCC officials blamed a combination of investigative hurdles and staffing shortages for the protracted review.

The inquiry was paused for years while the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) conducted its own investigation into Bauman’s arrest. In March 2024, it concluded that charges of unlawful confinement and assault should be considered against the three arresting officers.

Crown prosecutors, however, declined to lay charges, citing no reasonable likelihood of conviction — a decision Bauman’s parents condemned as another systemic failure that denied them access to justice.
“How do you continue on, and it's four years later with no repercussions?” Krause said. “We just want the officers held accountable.”
That May, the RCMP completed its own investigation and handed the findings over to the CRCC.
But the national watchdog found the RCMP review lacking and opted to investigate further, prolonging the timeline by months.

items: Alberta teen with autism still traumatized weeks after RCMP arrested him at a playground

blocks.text: Delays were further compounded because the watchdog lacked a permanent chairperson for more than a year, leaving hundreds of files stalled.
“We understand and sympathize with the Bauman family’s concerns over the timeline to complete the CRCC’s review and investigation,” commission officials said in a statement this week.
“We sincerely regret that the delays in this case have impacted Ryley and his family.”
'Justice delayed is justice denied'

The CRCC confirmed it received the RCMP’s response to its findings on Nov. 9, after CBC News inquired about the outstanding report. The CRCC said it now expects to release its final public report by the end of the year.

“The RCMP recognizes the significance of this matter for Ryley Bauman and his family and understands their desire for answers," RCMP national headquarters spokesperson Lisa McDonald-Bourg said in a statement to CBC News.
Tom Engel, chair of the Criminal Trial Lawyers' Association's (CTLA) policing committee, said the case demonstrates a long-overdue need for reform.
“It's typical of the delays in the RCMP Act disciplinary process,” Engel said. “Justice delayed is justice denied.”

items: No charges for RCMP officers who arrested non-verbal autistic teen at Alberta playground

blocks.text: Engel said the CTLA has advocated for decades for Ottawa to overhaul the RCMP Act and give the CRCC the statutory authority and resources required to conduct independent investigations and issue binding disciplinary orders.

Under the current framework, the watchdog rarely leads initial inquiries, relying instead on the RCMP to investigate, a process Engel criticized as lacking independence. The RCMP commissioner is also free to reject the commission's recommendations.
“The lack of teeth is a serious problem with the CRCC,” Engel said.

Ryley Bauman was arrested in October 2022 when police were called to a playground in St. Albert, Alta. An investigation found officers wrongfully identified the autistic teen as a known drug user. (Laura Hawthorne)
Amy Tint, a clinical psychologist who has researched how police interact with autistic people, said the delay in the investigation is disappointing.

Tint, an Azrieli Accelerator assistant professor in neurodiversity at the University of Calgary, said the Bauman investigation could provide critical insights into the training needed to ensure neurodivergent people are better protected when encountering police.
Her research has found that people who are neurodivergent are more likely to interact with police and are at greater risk.

“This family and this young person, I think they experienced a really traumatic experience that's having a lasting impact. And we know they're not alone, unfortunately. So it's an issue that we need to urgently address.”
'No going back'
The Bauman family has filed a lawsuit against the Attorney General of Canada, Alberta Health Services (AHS) and the lead arresting officer.
The suit seeks more than $15 million in damages for wrongful arrest and severe, ongoing psychological trauma, including PTSD and anxiety.
Court records show that AHS and the Attorney General of Canada have both asked that the case be dismissed.
In its statement of defence, the Attorney General of Canada rejected the family’s claims, denying any liability in the case and asserting that RCMP acted “in a reasonable manner.”
AHS also denied the allegations levied in the lawsuit, arguing in its statement of defence that the paramedics called to Bauman’s cell provided him emergency medical care in “good faith.”
Bauman’s parents said the civil proceedings remain largely on hold while they await the CRCC’s final report.
They say one reality remains inescapable: their son has been permanently altered and will now require lifelong, daily care.
Once happy and confident, Bauman now lives in a persistent state of fear and paranoia.
He’s been hospitalized since May, when his distress escalated, and his condition continues to deteriorate.
“They arrested a 16-year-old kid. They've destroyed his transition to adulthood,” Hawthorne said. “He's most likely turning 21 in a hospital bed… There is no going back.”

articles.title: Ombudsman on Romualdez's P560-M cash inflow: Where did it come from?
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Friday asked about the source of the P560 million in money transfers to former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez from 2022 to 2025, if they didn't come from…

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 7:39pm

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Friday asked about the source of the P560 million in money transfers to former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez from 2022 to 2025, if they didn't come from kickbacks related to flood control projects.

Remulla raised the question a day after Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) financial investigator Atty. Jan Mark Busa testified before Romualdez’s bail hearing that the P560.5 million worth of remittances were not related to flood control transactions.
Specifically, Busa said the remittances did not come from the Department of Public Works and Highways, any contractor, or then House Appropriations Panel Chair Zaldy Co.
Co is Romualdez’s co-accused in the P7.4 billion plunder case over his alleged involvement in the flood control kickback scheme.
“Saan nanggaling ‘yun? Saan nanggaling iyong pera? And AMLC is not necessarily the only one who knows where the money came from,” Remulla said.
(Where did that money come from?)
Asked if the AMLC witness's testimony affected the strength of the case against Romualdez, Remulla said, “Not at all.”
“Saka marami pa kaming testigo. Don’t worry about that,” he added.
(We still have other witnesses.)

Other co-accused of Romualdez and Co include Romualdez’s personal assistant Joselyn Tragua Sereño and Felicito Cristobal Guevarra, president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corporation, over their alleged links to the flood control kickback scheme. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys
articles.summary: The Spanish singer is recognised for her fourth album Lux which was released last year to rave reviews.

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Rosalía released her fourth album Lux last year to rave reviews
ByRiyah Collins
BBC Newsbeat
Spanish star Rosalía has made history as the first woman to win the best album award at the Latin Grammys three times, after being recognised for her project Lux.
The singer took home five trophies in total, including two for her track La Perla which was named song of the year and best pop song.
La Perla was also nominated for record of the year but missed out to Argentine singer Milo J's song Niño.

Rosalía released Lux last year to rave reviews and collecting her award at the ceremony in Las Vegas on Thursday, she said: "To all the people who told me I wasn't good enough, or that my music was too weird, I'm thankful I didn't listen."
The Barcelona-born artist then added: "Now I'm winning these prizes."
Rosalía, who opened the ceremony with a performance of some of her biggest songs, was honoured with the prize for best alternative music album.
She also picked up best shortform music video for her track Sauvignon Blanc.
The singer had previously won best album for El Mal Querer in 2019 and Motomami in 2022 - and her third Lux is also tipped to be a favourite when nominations are announced for the Grammys next week.

blocks.caption: Image caption, After a career spanning three decades, Daddy Yankee was recognised with a lifetime achievement award

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
After a career spanning three decades, Daddy Yankee was recognised with a lifetime achievement award
It was also a big night for Puerto Rican reggaeton legend Daddy Yankee, who won the person of the year award.
He performed some of his best-loved tracks including Gasolina and Con Calma, and was joined on stage by rappers including LL Cool J and French Montana.
Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh, who collabed with Daddy Yankee on Pokito, even took a break from his Aura India tour for the set, making him the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys.
Dosanjh superfan Devanshi Arora described the singer's appearance as "a cultural revolution".
"It's really invigorating and motivating to see someone from my country has made it all around the world," she tells Newsbeat.

articles.title: Nigerian university in mourning after four students die at post-exam party
articles.summary: The university has banned all parties, while investigations are underway to find the cause of the students' deaths.

blocks.text: Four Nigerian students have died after attending a party in the south-eastern town of Nsukka to celebrate the end of their final exams.
The cause of death has not been confirmed but police spokesman Daniel Ndukwe said the two men and two women had reportedly fallen ill after consuming alcoholic drinks at the party.
The University of Nigeria Nsukka has declared three days of mourning, during which academic and social activities will be suspended.
The tragedy comes amid a wider crackdown on fake and adulterated alcoholic drinks in Nigeria, where the food and drug regulator has been raiding suspected producers of unsafe food and beverages.

The university's Vice-Chancellor, Professor Simon Ortuanya, said the university had received a distress call at 22:00 on Wednesday, and sent security personnel to a house party at Praise Lodge, outside the campus in Nsukka's Hilltop area.
"The preliminary investigation and interim report point to alleged alcohol abuse or drug paraphernalia and things like that. But we are not conclusive on those matters," he said.
He described the deaths as "tragic and painful".
"As a community, we mourn, not just alone, we mourn with the families, the parents that have suffered these years to train the men and women in their studies," he said.
Ortuanya also announced a ban on signing-out celebrations, which are commonly held by final-year students to mark the completion of their studies.

The celebrations often involve parties, dancing, photographs and friends signing one another's shirts. He urged students to use graduation as a time to reflect on their university experience and prepare for life beyond campus.
The university said it was working with security agencies to establish what had caused the deaths.
The police have also launched an investigation. They said alcoholic drinks had been recovered from the scene and the bodies taken to a mortuary for autopsies.
The investigation comes amid wider concerns about unsafe alcoholic drinks in Nigeria.
In September, dozens of people fell ill after consuming locally made alcoholic drinks and herbal mixtures in communities across Ondo State, south-west Nigeria.
More than 11 people died in the Araromi-Obu area, while more than 50 others were hospitalised.
Investigations found that some of the drinks had been contaminated with methanol, a highly toxic form of alcohol that can cause blindness and death.
Nigeria's food and drug regulator, Nafdac, reported more than 150 cases, including 48 confirmed deaths. More than 80 people were hospitalised, and five lost their sight.
The regulator has been carrying out raids across the country, targeting facilities suspected of producing fake or adulterated alcoholic drinks, food and beverages.
Nigeria has long struggled with the sale of unsafe and adulterated products, which campaigners warn pose a serious threat to public health.

articles.title: What’s behind Australia’s surge in teen extremism?
articles.summary:
Young people are being found with ‘hard drives full of what can only be described as gore’, one expert says

  • Get our

blocks.text: In March, Guardian Australia revealed that most people who have been charged with the new federal crime of possession of violent extremist material are under 18.
This week Australian federal police sounded the alarm about a surge in teen extremism: 32 of the 37 young people prosecuted in counter-terrorism cases since 2020 were charged in the past two years.

The growth in youth extremism is happening within a sprawling online ecosystem. My investigations have tracked the rise of online networks that urge violence and nihilism for their own sake, in which perpetrators coerce victims not much younger than themselves to commit brutal and degrading acts.

In a review of 55 youth terrorism cases, the AFP has found that the profile is mixed. They are often young men. Many have received some support or intervention for a mental health condition. Some are from stable homes, others not.
What they have most in common is that they are young people on the internet. Experts say the age of those caught up in these crimes is decreasing.
In the last month two teenagers in Darwin have been charged with collecting documents that could facilitate acts of terrorism.

The arrests came five months after another NT teenager was charged with making posts with “pro-Nazi, anti-immigration, anti-trans and white nationalist themes”. The charge sheet alleges he also possessed videos of white nationalist terrorist attacks, including the 2019 Christchurch mosque shooting and the 2022 Buffalo shooting that it partly inspired.
All matters are still before the courts.
Experts involved in harm prevention programs, including the Victoria University professor Debra Smith, have watched the age of this cohort decrease dramatically over the past decade.

Instead of considering the challenge exclusively through the lens of radicalisation, Smith says we need to recognise that some young people are being socialised and finding identity in online spaces that may appear exciting and transgressive but are ultimately harmful to themselves, and may encourage them to do harm to others.
She has seen cases where teenagers are being found with “hard drives full of what can only be described as gore”.

“It’s like getting involved in any other … unhealthy subcultural aspect of life … [such as] gangs or crime for payment,” she says. “There’s this offering of what young people can look at and get involved in that just simply wasn’t there years ago.”

The Guardian’s investigation into the growth of extremist material charges, as well as the surge of young people in Australia ensnared in sadistic online extortion and gore networks, reveals an amorphous online ecosystem in which young people may easily come into contact with extreme and violent content.

A teenager in New South Wales who pleaded guilty to possessing violent extremist material, among other charges, described how he first came across such content on TikTok when he was 14 and sought validation by talking to others online. He used ChatGPT to research the Boston marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev as well as security arrangements at the Sydney Opera House. He was sentenced to a three-year community corrections order.
Others have told police how they became involved in so-called “gore” channels on Telegram, where more and more extreme footage – including of animal abuse – is traded.

Given the age of many involved, Levi West, a research fellow at the Australian National University, says they may be considered as much victims as perpetrators, which is a significant challenge for how authorities respond.
after newsletter promotion

It’s important for parents, schools and others to think about what’s sitting underneath the uptick in numbers, he says, and not just the “algorithms”. He points to the legacies of Covid-19 and lockdowns as well as the presence of screens and digital technologies in the lives of young people.
“We are not going to arrest our way out of this problem,” West says.
With people as young as 13 before the courts, Australia must consider if authorities are taking the right approach and have the right resources for this challenge.

The Guardian’s investigation into the possession of extremist material charges in South Australia and around the country found that many of those who had been before the courts faced a range of health and social difficulties, including autism diagnoses and learning challenges – and raised questions about whether some young people understand a crime has been committed.
Smith has seen many young people caught up in these activities who come from troubled family backgrounds, while others have had every opportunity in life.

There is a role for everyone involved in caring for young people, she says, from parents and schools to sporting clubs, to recognise when someone might be engaging in harmful behaviours long before there is a risk of violence, then help them access non-punitive pathways for help.
“It’s really important to understand it through a developmental lens – that these are young people who are making decisions with young brains,” Smith says.
“My grave concern is that if we are just giving everyone terrorism offences at [age] 12, 13, 14, 15, we’re starting to label them the thing that they will become.”
